title: Command line
text:
# Command line

## Synopsis

```text
nurt -V | --version
nurt -h | --help
nurt <program>
nurt exec [--variant a|b|c] [--preview] [--json | --format F] [--limit N] [--cursor C] [--verbosity V] [--privilege P] [--as-user NAME] <program>
nurt script <file.nurt> [--preview]
nurt check <file.nurt | -e '<program>'>
nurt fmt <file.nurt> [--variant a|b|c]
nurt ast [--from a|b|c|json] [--to json|cbor|a|b|c] <input>
nurt schema ast|bound|report|request|config|tool
nurt schema tool [--format <format>] [--language en|pl] [--groups core|all|<group>,<group>...]
nurt catalog [command | group]
nurt help [topic]
nurt history|undo|redo [arguments]
nurt serve --stdio | --socket <path>
nurt mcp [--stdio | --http <address>]
nurt lsp
nurt migrate <file.sh | file.ps1>
nurt service install|uninstall|start|stop|status|run
nurt journal salvage <volume>
nurt ext install|remove|list
nurt doctor
nurt version
```

## Description

`nurt` is a command shell and language where every change can be undone.

`nurt` runs programs of the Danaco Nurt language and serves the engine to other programs. A first argument that is not a subcommand is a program: `nurt run ["go", "test"] cwd: "/home/user/app"`. `nurt exec` is always unambiguous.

The options with `--` belong to the program `nurt`. The language has no options with a hyphen; the corrections translate such habits.

## Options

| Option | Function |
|---|---|
| `-V` | prints `nurt <version>` |
| `--version` | prints `nurt <version> (<commit> <date>)`, the copyright line and the license |
| `-h`, `--help` | prints the help; the first line is the description of the program |

The output of `--version` has three lines. The part in parentheses is omitted when the executable is built without repository data.

```text
nurt <version> (<commit> <date>)
Copyright (c) 2026 Danaco Holding Group Sp. z o.o. All rights reserved.
License: Apache-2.0
```

## Subcommands

| Subcommand | Function |
|---|---|
| `exec` | runs a program from the argument |
| `script` | runs the pipelines of a file one after another; each pipeline is a separate operation |
| `repl` | interactive session with history, completion of names and parameters, and job control |
| `check` | parses, corrects and binds a program, prints the canonical form, changes nothing |
| `fmt` | prints a file in canonical form |
| `ast` | converts a program between the text variants and the syntax tree formats |
| `schema` | prints a JSON schema, or the definition of the tool for an AI platform |
| `catalog` | prints the catalog, a group or one command |
| `help` | built-in help |
| `history`, `undo`, `redo` | shortcuts for the journal commands |
| `serve` | JSON-RPC server `nurt-rpc/1` for a host program |
| `mcp` | Model Context Protocol server that provides the tool `nurt` |
| `lsp` | language server for `.nurt` files |
| `migrate` | translates a shell script into a `.nurt` file |
| `service` | manages the background service of the journal |
| `journal salvage` | repairs entries marked `corrupt` |
| `ext` | manages extensions |
| `doctor` | reports file system properties, permissions, the service, versions and language servers |
| `version` | prints the version |

## Environment

Variables with the prefix `NURT_` set configuration keys; see [Configuration](configuration.md). `NURT_CONFIG` names an additional configuration file.

## Files

The system, user and project configuration files and the state directory are listed in [Configuration](configuration.md).

## See also

`nurt-commands(7)`, `nurt-<command>(1)`

title: Compatibility
text:
# Compatibility

## License and names

The source code is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, and distributions include the file `NOTICE`. The specification and the data sets are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The license does not grant permission to use the names "Danaco" and "Danaco Nurt" beyond the customary description of the origin of the product. See [LICENSE](https://github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt/blob/main/LICENSE) and [NOTICE](https://github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt/blob/main/NOTICE).

## Danaco Nurt Compatible

An implementation or an integration that passes the mandatory tests of `nurt-conformance` may use the name "Danaco Nurt Compatible" and the mark of the program. The terms of the program are published after they are approved by the owner of the name.

title: Configuration
text:
# Configuration

The format is `nurt-config/1`. The complete list of keys with types and defaults is in the [specification](../../spec/configuration.md); the schema is printed by `nurt schema config`.

## Files

| System | System file | User file | State directory |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux | `/etc/nurt/nurt.toml` | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nurt/nurt.toml` (default `~/.config/nurt/nurt.toml`) | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/nurt/` |
| macOS | `/Library/Application Support/Nurt/nurt.toml` | `~/Library/Application Support/Nurt/nurt.toml` | `~/Library/Application Support/Nurt/` |
| Windows | `%PROGRAMDATA%\Nurt\nurt.toml` | `%APPDATA%\Nurt\nurt.toml` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Nurt\` |

A project may contain `.nurt.toml`.

## Precedence

Later levels override earlier ones:

1. built-in defaults
2. the system file
3. the user file
4. `.nurt.toml` of the project
5. the file named by `NURT_CONFIG`
6. the variables `NURT_*`
7. the parameters of the call

## Project files

`.nurt.toml` may set `scope.base`, `scope.project_roots`, `report.*` and `run.*`, and `journal.*` for trusted projects only. The keys `scope.trusted_projects`, `scope.trust*` and `service.*` in a project file are ignored and reported as `trust_config_ignored`.

## Keys used in the documentation

| Key | Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `syntax.variant` | `NURT_SYNTAX` | `a` | variant of the text syntax |
| `syntax.tolerant` | `NURT_SYNTAX_TOLERANT` | `true` | accept the syntax of the other variants |
| `correction.enabled` | `NURT_CORRECTION` | `true` | corrections of the form |
| `journal.enabled` | `NURT_JOURNAL` | `true` | journal of changes |
| `journal.max_ops` | `NURT_JOURNAL_MAX_OPS` | `30` | operations kept |
| `journal.max_age` | `NURT_JOURNAL_MAX_AGE` | `"30m"` | age of the operations kept |
| `run.timeout` | `NURT_RUN_TIMEOUT` | `"120s"` | time limit of `run` |
| `output.language` | `NURT_LANGUAGE` | `"en"` | language of `help`, `describe`, the messages of errors and the notes of a result (`en` or `pl`); codes and programs are never translated |
| `output.color` | `NURT_COLOR` | `"auto"` | colors for a person |
| `session.id` | `NURT_SESSION` | none | session identifier in the journal |

title: Effect report
text:
# Effect report

Each run returns a description of the effect, not only the fact that something ran. The format is `nurt-report/1`; the schema and the complete field list are in the [specification](../../spec/report.md).

## Status

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | the program ran and the effect was applied |
| `planned` | a preview computed the targets and the effect; nothing changed |
| `partial` | the effect was applied to part of the targets; `irreversible` or `error` lists the rest |
| `failed` | the program failed; the member `error` describes it |

## Fields

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `op` | number of the journal entry of the operation; absent for reading programs and previews |
| `targets` | number of files, directories and bytes that the program touched |
| `changes` | changed targets on the current page |
| `notable` | unusual effects such as `mass_delete`, `size_shrunk` or `nothing_matched` |
| `irreversible` | effects that undo cannot reverse |
| `records` | result of a reading program: record type, number of matches and rows |
| `error` | code, message, stage, position and corrections of a failed program |

## Verbosity and paging

The call parameter `verbosity` selects `quiet`, `normal` or `detailed`. `limit` sets the number of records or changes on a page and `cursor` reads the next page; reading a page again never runs a changing program again. A response that leaves lines, records or the end of long lines out carries the field `continuation` and its text ends with `more: next`; the command `next` returns the next part (`next 200`, `next all`, `next full`). `format` selects `text`, `json`, `markdown` or `compact`.

## Operations on many targets

An operation with 200 or more targets is a bulk operation. The description shows the extensions, the first and last targets and the unusual effects, and the full list is available through the cursor.

## Errors

An error carries a stable code. [Error codes](../../spec/errors.md) lists the codes, the stage that reports each and the status of the C interface.

title: First steps
text:
# First steps

## Running a program

`nurt` takes a program as its argument. A program is a command with arguments, optionally followed by more commands joined with `|>`.

```nurt example
find "/home/user/app" glob: "**/*.go" |> filter size > 1mb |> sort size order: desc |> first 5
```

The command `find` produces `entry` records, one for each file. `filter`, `sort` and `first` consume and produce records of the same kind. The text of the result lists the remaining records.

## Paths and arguments

A path is a quoted text: `"/home/user/app"` or `"C:/Users/user/app"`. A regular expression is written between slashes: `/oldName\(/`. A name followed by a colon introduces a named argument: `glob: "**/*.go"`. Positional arguments follow the order of the parameters on the page of the command.

## Checking before running

`nurt check` parses a program, applies the corrections of the language and binds it to the catalog. It prints the canonical form and the effect, and changes nothing.

```text
nurt check -e 'remove "/home/user/app/build"'
```

The call parameter `preview: true` runs a changing program without changing anything and reports the targets.

## Reading the report

A program that changes files returns an effect report: the status, the number of the operation in the journal, the targets, the changes and any unusual effects. [Effect report](effect-report.md) lists the fields.

```nurt example
replace /oldName\(/ "newName(" in: ["/home/user/app/src"] glob: "**/*.go"
```

## Undoing a change

Every operation that changes files is recorded in the journal. `history` lists the operations and `undo` reverses one of them.

```nurt example
undo 18
```

See [Journal and undo](journal.md) for conflicts, retention and the operations that cannot be reversed.

## Getting help

`help` without arguments lists the commands. `help <command>` shows the synopsis, the parameters, the record kinds, the effect and examples.

```nurt example
help "replace"
```

title: Danaco Nurt
text:
# Danaco Nurt

Danaco Nurt (`nurt`) is a command shell and language where every change can be undone.

The language works with files, text, structured documents, source code, version control, processes and the operating system. A program is a pipeline of typed records. Each program is checked before it runs, and each run returns a report of its effects.

The command line program `nurt` runs programs in a terminal and in scripts. Other programs call the same engine as a tool through the Model Context Protocol, a JSON-RPC server or a library.

## Documentation

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| [Installation](installation.md) | Obtaining and verifying the executable |
| [First steps](first-steps.md) | Running a program, reading a result, undoing a change |
| [Language](language.md) | Syntax, values, pipelines and corrections |
| [Command line](command-line.md) | The `nurt` program and its subcommands |
| [Effect report](effect-report.md) | Fields of the report of a run |
| [Journal and undo](journal.md) | Recording, undoing and redoing changes |
| [Configuration](configuration.md) | Files, levels and keys |
| [Integration](integration.md) | Tool definitions, MCP and libraries |
| [Commands](../commands/README.md) | One page for each of the 177 commands |
| [Cookbook](../cookbook/README.md) | Programs for common tasks |
| [Cheat sheets](../cheatsheets/nurt-for-bash-users.md) | Habits of bash and PowerShell and their forms in Nurt |
| [Specification](../../spec/catalog.md) | Language, catalog, report, journal and configuration |
| [Compatibility](compatibility.md) | Names and the Danaco Nurt Compatible program |
| [Versioning and support](versioning.md) | Versions, deprecation and supported systems |
| [Security](security.md) | Reporting vulnerabilities and the security model |

## Commands

The catalog has 177 commands. The 34 core commands cover files, text, records, programs, the journal and help. The other commands belong to 14 optional groups such as `git`, `code`, `archive` and `network`.

title: Installation
text:
# Installation

Danaco Nurt is one executable for each operating system: `nurt` on Linux and macOS, `nurt.exe` on Windows. The executable has no runtime dependencies.

## Supported systems

| System | Architectures |
|---|---|
| Linux | x86_64, aarch64 |
| macOS | x86_64, aarch64 |
| Windows | x86_64, aarch64 |

## Release artifacts

| Channel | Identifier |
|---|---|
| GitHub release | `github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt` |
| Container image | `ghcr.io/danacoofficial/nurt` |
| winget | `Danaco.Nurt` |
| NuGet (library binding) | `Danaco.Nurt` |
| Maven (library binding) | `pl.danaco-group:nurt` |

Every release publishes SHA-256 sums of its artifacts. The installers `install.sh` and `install.ps1` verify the sum before they place the executable.

## Install on Linux and macOS

```text
curl -fsSL https://nurt.danaco-group.pl/install.sh | sh
```

The script installs `nurt` into `$HOME/.local/bin` and needs no privileges. On Linux it takes the static musl archive when the release has one and the glibc archive otherwise. For a system-wide installation run the script as root with `--bin-dir /usr/local/bin`. The option `--public-key` verifies the signature of `checksums.txt`; the key and the procedure are in `SECURITY.md`.

## Install on Windows

```text
irm https://nurt.danaco-group.pl/install.ps1 | iex
```

By default the script installs for the current user. `nurt.exe` goes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Nurt\bin`, the documentation to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Nurt\doc`, and the directory of the executable is added to the `PATH` of the user. No administrator privileges are needed.

To install for all users, start PowerShell with "Run as administrator" and set the scope before the call:

```text
$env:NURT_SCOPE = 'machine'
irm https://nurt.danaco-group.pl/install.ps1 | iex
```

The scope `machine` installs into `%ProgramFiles%\Nurt` and changes the `PATH` of the machine. The variable `NURT_INSTALL_DIR` selects another directory for the executable.

### Administrator rights

`nurt.exe` does not ask for elevation. Its manifest declares the execution level `asInvoker`, so the program runs with the rights of the terminal that starts it. Operations that need administrator rights, such as `nurt service install`, changes in the machine part of the registry and writes to system directories, work in a terminal that runs as administrator. The manifest also declares long path support and UTF-8 as the code page of the process.

## Contents of the archives

| Archive | Files |
|---|---|
| Program, Linux and macOS, directory `nurt-<version>-<target>/` | `nurt`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `man/`, `completions/`, `doc/` |
| Program, Windows, files at the top level | `nurt.exe`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `completions/`, `doc/` |
| C library, Linux and macOS, directory `nurt-lib-<version>-<target>/` | `libnurt.so.1` or `libnurt.1.dylib`, `nurt.h`, `nurt.pc`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` |
| C library, Linux musl, directory `nurt-lib-<version>-<target>/` | `libnurt.a` (static), `nurt.h`, `nurt.pc`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` |
| C library, Windows, files at the top level | `nurt.dll`, `nurt.h`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` |

The C library archives are published for the targets that have a library; the installers `install.sh` and `install.ps1` install the program archive only.

The directory `doc/` holds this documentation as a site that works offline; open `doc/index.html`. The directory `completions/` holds the completion scripts for Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell and Elvish.

## Build from source

The build needs a Rust toolchain installed with rustup and a C compiler. The toolchain version is pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`.

```text
git clone https://github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt.git
cd nurt
cargo build --release --locked
```

The executable is written to `target/release/nurt` (`target\release\nurt.exe` on Windows).

## Verification

```text
nurt --version
```

The command prints the version, the copyright line and the license; the format is described in [Command line](command-line.md). `nurt doctor` reports the properties of the file system, the permissions, the service and the language servers that it found.

## License

The product is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. Distributions include the `NOTICE` file. See [Compatibility](compatibility.md) for the use of the name.

title: Integration
text:
# Integration

A host program can call Danaco Nurt in four ways. The tool seen by a model is named `nurt` in every integration.

| Interface | Use |
|---|---|
| MCP server | `nurt mcp --stdio` or `nurt mcp --http <address>` provides the tool `nurt` |
| JSON-RPC | `nurt serve --stdio` or `nurt serve --socket <path>` speaks `nurt-rpc/1` |
| C library | `libnurt` and `nurt.h`; the bindings for other languages use it |
| Rust library | the crate `nurt-core` |

## The tool

The tool takes a program in text, or a syntax tree, and returns the effect report. The schema of the tool is `nurt-tool/1`; `nurt schema tool` prints it. The definition of the tool for a platform, with the description for the model, is produced by the console from the catalog with `nurt schema tool --format <format>`, so it always agrees with the installed version.

```text
nurt schema tool
nurt schema tool --format anthropic
```

## Policies of the engine

The command `nurt check` and the library function `nurt_check` return the effects, paths, targets, external programs, network hosts and groups of a program without running it. An engine applies its own permission policy to this result before it calls the tool.

## Documentation for integrators

The guide for integrators, with tool definitions for the model providers and examples of policies, is the directory [docs/integrators](https://github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt/tree/main/docs/integrators) of the repository.

title: Journal and undo
text:
# Journal and undo

The journal records every operation that changes files, together with the previous content that undo needs. The contract is in the [specification](../../spec/journal.md).

## Commands

| Command | Function |
|---|---|
| `history` | lists operations; filters by state, path and range |
| `undo` | reverses one operation, the operations since a point, or the changes of given files |
| `redo` | applies an undone operation again |
| `journal.status` | shows whether the journal is on and what it holds |
| `journal.space` | shows free space and the space held by the journal |
| `journal.limits` | sets retention for the session or the user |
| `journal.pin` | keeps an entry beyond the retention limits |
| `journal.purge` | removes entries |

```nurt example
history limit: 5
```

## Entry states

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `available` | the entry can be undone |
| `partial` | part of the preserved content was released to free disk space |
| `expired` | the entry left the retention window |
| `undone` | the entry was undone |

## Undo conflicts

When a file changed after the operation, `undo` reports `E_JOURNAL_CONFLICT` with the file and the hashes. The parameter `on_conflict` chooses `force`, `include_later`, `partial` or `abort`; the default `report` changes nothing.

```nurt example
undo 18 on_conflict: include_later
```

## Retention

The defaults keep the last 30 operations and the operations of the last 30 minutes. The keys `journal.max_ops`, `journal.max_age` and `journal.max_size` change the limits; see [Configuration](configuration.md). An operation whose previous content was not preserved is reported as `irreversible` with the reason.

## Crash safety

An operation on many targets is one journal entry. After a power loss the recovery step rolls back an entry that was not committed.

title: Language
text:
# Language

The language is defined by the specification: [syntax tree](../../spec/syntax-tree.md), [catalog](../../spec/catalog.md), [records](../../spec/records.md) and [stages](../../spec/stages.md). This page summarizes the rules that the documentation uses.

## Programs and pipelines

A program is a sequence of statements separated by line breaks. A statement is a pipeline or a `let` binding. A pipeline is a command followed by commands joined with `|>`. A line break before `|>` continues the pipeline.

```nurt example
let recent = find "/home/user/app/src" glob: "**/*.ts" |> filter modified > ago(1h)
@recent |> count
```

`let name = pipeline` stores the result under a name and `@name` uses it. There are no variables in text and no substitution of `$` in values.

## Values

| Kind | Written as | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Text | double quotes, escapes `\n \t \\ \"` | `"/home/user/app"` |
| Raw text | `r"…"` or `r#"…"#` | `r#"import "fmt""#` |
| Regular expression | between slashes, flags `i m s x` | `/oldName\(/i` |
| Integer, number | digits, `_` allowed | `1_000`, `1.5` |
| Size | number and unit `b kb mb gb tb kib mib gib tib` | `10mb` |
| Duration | numbers with units `ms s m h d w` | `1h30m` |
| Range | `5`, `1..5`, `40..`, `..9`, `all` | `10..20` |
| List, map | brackets, braces | `["a", "b"]`, `{CI: "1"}` |
| Boolean, null | `true`, `false`, `null` | `true` |

A size written with decimal units (`mb`) counts 1 000 000 bytes for `1mb`; a binary unit (`mib`) counts 1 048 576 bytes.

## Arguments

Positional arguments follow the order of the positions in the catalog. Named arguments are written `name: value` and may appear anywhere after the positional ones. Parameters have types; the [type grammar](../../spec/catalog.md) lists them.

## Expressions

`filter`, `sort`, `select`, `assert` and `evaluate` take expressions evaluated on each record. Operators are `== != < <= > >= ~ !~ in and or not + - * /`. `~` matches a regular expression. Functions include `ago(duration)`.

## Conditions

`when` runs one branch. The condition is a `bool` expression: comparisons, `and`, `or`, `not`, `exists <path>`, a reading pipeline in parentheses (`(processes name: "nginx" |> count) > 0`), `exit_code` and the fields of a record held by a `let`. `otherwise when` repeats and `otherwise` is optional. The condition is evaluated once, before its branch; the report gives its value and the number of the branch. A condition that is not `bool` is `E_TYPE` before any effect when its type is known at binding: a comparison, a bare pipeline, `exit_code`, and a field of the loop record whose type the output record of the source command declares. The same holds for every use of such a field that no value of its type can satisfy: `f.size ~ "x"`, `f.name < 3`, `f.name == 3`, `not f.name`, `f.path - 1`, `1 in f.size`. The only exception is a field typed `any` or `json`, whose type depends on the data: it is checked when the condition is evaluated, and a failure then restores the construct. A pipeline in a condition only reads: a stage that may change the world and takes its action from a value that is not a literal (`http.request … method: @m`, `git.branch delete: @a`) is `E_TYPE` at binding.

```nurt example
when (read "/etc/app.toml" key: "mode") == "prod" {
    replace /debug = true/ "debug = false" in: "/etc/app.toml" expect: 1
} otherwise when exists "/srv/app/.staging" {
    write "/srv/app/.ready" "staging\n" mode: overwrite
} otherwise {
    write "/srv/app/.dev" "1\n" mode: overwrite
}
```

## Loops

`each <records> as name { … }` runs the block once per record, in order; `name` is the record and `name.path` a field. `repeat until: <bool> every: <duration> limit: <duration or number> { … }` runs the block and then tests the condition; `while <bool> limit: <duration or number> { … }` tests before each run. Without `limit` a loop ends at `loop.max_iterations` (10 000) or `loop.max_time` (10 minutes): `repeat` then ends with `E_LIMIT`, `while` ends normally and the report says that the limit ended it. With `limit` the loop ignores the configured defaults: a number of iterations is then not bounded by time, and a duration is not bounded by the number of iterations. `preview` plans one iteration of a `repeat` or a `while`, because the number of iterations is known only by running; an `each` plans every iteration. `and` and `or` evaluate both operands, so a pipeline in the right operand also runs when the left one decides. `break` and `continue` work inside a loop, usually after `when`. `each` accepts `parallel: N`; every loop accepts `atomic: false`, which keeps the iterations completed before a failure and names the failed one.

```nurt example
each (find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.log") as f {
    lines f.path |> filter text ~ /ERROR/ |> write "/srv/reports/" + f.name + ".err" mode: overwrite
}
```

## Several changes in one call

`steps { … }` holds pipelines that each change; `let` passes results to later steps.

```nurt example
steps {
    find "/srv/app/old" glob: "*.conf" |> move to: "/srv/app/conf"
    replace /old\/path/ "conf/path" in: "/srv/app/app.toml" expect: 3
}
```

## Functions

`define name(parameter: type = default, …) { … }` defines a function; a call is written `name(value, parameter: value)`. The body sees its parameters (`@dir`) and its own `let`, nothing of the caller. The value of the last statement is the result. Recursion ends with `E_LIMIT` at `function.max_depth` (64).

```nurt example
define rotate_logs(dir: path, keep: int = 7) {
    find @dir glob: "*.log.*" |> sort modified desc |> skip @keep |> remove
}
rotate_logs("/var/log/app1")
rotate_logs("/var/log/app2", keep: 14)
```

## Script parameters

A file starts with `params { … }`; each line is a name, a type and an optional default. `nurt run cleanup.nurt dir: "/srv/app" days: 7 dry` passes the values, `nurt run cleanup.nurt --help` prints the declaration, and the engine takes the values in the `params` member of the request. A missing value, an unknown name (with the nearest name) or a value of the wrong type is reported before anything runs.

```nurt example
params {
    dir: path
    days: int = 30
    dry: bool = false
}
find @dir glob: "**/*.log" |> filter modified < ago(@days * 1d) |> remove preview: @dry
```

## Rules of every construct

A construct is one journal entry: one `undo` reverses all of it. It is all or nothing: when a part fails, the changes already made are rolled back, and the parts that cannot be rolled back (a program run, a restart) are listed before the change and named in the error. `preview` computes the chosen branch, the iterations and every effect without a change. Types, names and arity are checked before any effect, and constructs are part of the syntax tree: no text is evaluated.

## Boolean shorthand

A parameter of type `bool` written without a value is `true`: `remove "/tmp/x" preview`, `nurt run cleanup.nurt dry`. `false` is always written out (`preview: false`). A parameter that is not `bool` written without a value is `E_MISSING_PARAM` with the expected type.

## Corrections

Nurt accepts the habits of other shells and forms with small errors. A correction changes the form of the program and never its meaning. Corrections that touch a target of a change are reported with ranked candidates instead of being applied. The habits of bash and PowerShell and the form of each in Nurt are listed on the cheat sheets for [bash](../cheatsheets/nurt-for-bash-users.md) and [PowerShell](../cheatsheets/nurt-for-powershell-users.md).

## Errors

An error has a stable code such as `E_UNKNOWN_PARAM`, a message and, where known, the stage, the position and a replacement program. [Error codes](../../spec/errors.md) lists the codes.

## Choosing a construct

| The task | Write | Journal and failure |
|---|---|---|
| one change | a pipeline with one changing stage at its end | one entry |
| several changes that stand or fall together | `steps { … }` | one entry, all or nothing |
| a change that depends on the state found | `when … otherwise …` | one entry with the chosen branch |
| the same change for many records | `each … as name { … }` | one entry; `atomic: false` keeps the completed iterations |
| poll for a state, or repeat until a limit | `repeat until:` or `while`, with `limit` | one entry; the limit ends with `E_LIMIT` in `repeat` |
| a change used several times in a file | `define name(…) { … }` | part of the entry of the caller |
| a file that takes values | `params { … }`, then `nurt run file.nurt name: value` | checked before any effect |

A single pipeline that has more than one changing stage is `E_ONE_EFFECT`; the correction proposes the same pipelines inside `steps` as the first candidate. The mode `script: true` stays for scripts that want a separate journal entry for every pipeline.

## Where the other features are described

- `sql` changes a database without `write: true`, accepts `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `ATTACH`, `VACUUM` and `VACUUM INTO`, and journals every database file it changes: see the [command](../commands/sql.md).
- `create` makes named pipes (`type: fifo`) and device nodes (`type: device`): see the [guide for Linux and macOS](../guides/unix.md).
- Accounts, groups, mounts, kernel parameters, firewall, network, clock, power and disks, and elevated work with `privilege` and `as_user`: see the [administration guide](../guides/administration.md).
- The habits of bash and PowerShell and their form in Nurt: see the guides for [bash](../guides/bash-migration.md) and [PowerShell](../guides/powershell-migration.md).

title: Security
text:
# Security

## Reporting a vulnerability

Suspected vulnerabilities are reported by e-mail to `support@danaco-group.pl` with a subject that starts with `[security] nurt`, not in a public issue. The policy, the scope and the handling times are in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/DanacoOfficial/danaco-nurt/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Properties of the shell

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| Check before effect | Names, parameters and types are validated against the catalog before any effect takes place |
| No shell | Programs do not pass through a shell; a path is one value and is not split or expanded |
| One effect per program | A program with more than one changing or running command is rejected with `E_ONE_EFFECT` |
| Report | Each run reports its targets, unusual effects and irreversible effects |
| Journal | Changes to files are recorded and can be undone within the retention limits |
| Secrets | Parameters marked `secret` in the catalog are masked in the journal, the report and printed trees |
| Project files | A project file cannot grant itself trust; the keys that widen trust are ignored in `.nurt.toml` |

## Privilege elevation

A call may ask for the rights of the administrator with the call parameter `privilege` (`account`, `elevated`, `auto`) and for another account with `as_user`. Nurt applies no policy of its own: the decision belongs to the embedding engine, which sets `privilege.allowed = false` to refuse `elevated` and `auto` with `E_PRIVILEGE` and the reason `disabled_by_configuration`. A project file cannot set `privilege.*`.

| Backend | How it works |
|---|---|
| `self` | the process already is the administrator; the operation runs in the same process |
| `sudo`, `doas`, `run0` | `nurt elevated-exec` is started with the rights of the administrator and reads one request in the request format of the protocol on its standard input; no shell text is built and no password is asked (`-n`, `nopass`, `--no-ask-password`) |
| `broker` | the privileged service `nurt-elevation`; reported as `not_installed` until it is released |

The order and the set of backends come from `privilege.backends`. Access control is that of the operating system: an account that may run `nurt` through `sudo`, `doas` or `run0` is administrator-equivalent, as with those programs. The elevated process refuses to run unless its identity is the administrator (or the account named by `as_user`), writes its journal entry to the journal of the account that asked, with the rights of that account (on Linux through the file system identity of the thread, on macOS through descriptors that are checked and handed to the account with `fchown` before anything is written; on Windows it is the same account), and returns the report, which states `elevated: true` and the `backend`.

The properties that matter for a permission policy of a host program are returned by `nurt check`; see [Integration](integration.md).

title: Versioning and support
text:
# Versioning and support

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| Program | Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. Releases of one major version do not break compatibility. Minor releases appear every 8 weeks and patch releases as needed |
| Language | `language MAJOR.MINOR`. Within a major version the language only grows. Synonyms and aliases of the corrections are kept. A deprecation is marked in `help` and the removal comes no earlier than 24 months later, in a major version |
| Syntax tree | `nurt-ast/MAJOR`. A new minor version only adds. The previous major version is accepted for 24 months |
| C interface | `NURT_ABI_MAJOR.MINOR` and the library name `libnurt.so.<MAJOR>`. Within a major version functions are only added |
| Catalog | The catalog only grows within `nurt-catalog/1`: new commands, new optional parameters with a default that keeps the previous behavior, new enumeration values. Removing or renaming a command or parameter, or changing a type or default, is a change of the major version |
| Long-term support | One release a year is a long-term support release. It receives fixes of defects and vulnerabilities for 36 months and no new features |

## Supported systems

Linux (x86_64, aarch64), macOS (x86_64, aarch64) and Windows (x86_64, aarch64).

## Support

Questions and defects are reported to `support@danaco-group.pl`. Vulnerabilities follow [Security](security.md).

title: administration
text:
# administration

## Boundaries

Administration commands read the state of the system and, in some cases, change it. Changes need the rights of the administrator more often than other work, so the call parameter `privilege` is part of the language, and changes outside the file system have inverse operations.

## Elevated work

Work that needs the rights of the administrator takes the call parameter `privilege`: `account` (the default) runs with the rights of the account, `elevated` runs with those of the administrator, and `auto` runs with the account and repeats the whole stage once with `elevated` when a target fails with `E_PERMISSION` or `E_PRIVILEGE`, before any change is kept. `as_user: "NAME"` runs the operation as another account on Linux and macOS. Both are written on a stage (`write "/etc/hosts" "..." privilege: elevated`), given in the request, or set on the command line with `--privilege` and `--as-user`; the configuration key `privilege.default` sets the value for calls that give none. Nurt starts `sudo`, `doas` or `run0` (or runs in the same process when it already is the administrator), sends the syntax tree of the program, never shell text, and never asks for a password: a backend that would ask is reported as `password_required`. The report of the operation states `elevated: true`, the `backend` and, for `auto`, the `elevation_reason`. When no backend can run the operation, the call ends with `E_PRIVILEGE`; its detail `backend` lists every backend with its result and `next_steps` names the way forward. The embedding engine switches elevation off with `privilege.allowed = false`.

## Elevated entries in the journal

Elevated entries are in the journal of the account, and the account has access to their copies; `undo N` and `redo N` of such an entry restore the targets through the same backend; `undo` and `redo` without a number that would restore an elevated entry end with `E_PRIVILEGE` and the next step `undo N privilege: elevated`. The elevated process writes the journal of the account with the rights of the account on Linux and macOS; on Windows the backend `self` is the same account.

## Undo of changes outside the file system

Changes outside the file system are undone by inverse operations that the engine derives from the state recorded in the report:

| Operation | Undo |
|---|---|
| `package.install` | `package.remove` when the package was not installed before; reinstall of the recorded version when the version changed |
| `package.remove` | `package.install` of the recorded version, when the repository still offers it |
| `package.upgrade` | install of the recorded versions, when the repository still offers them |
| `start`, `stop` | the opposite command |
| `enable`, `disable` | the opposite command with the recorded start type |

`enable` and `disable` are undone only for the start types `disabled` and `automatic`; other start types make the entry irreversible, with the reason in the report. A package version that the repository no longer offers makes only that package irreversible.

Irreversible are `restart`, `stop` of a process, and `run`: files changed by a program started with `run` and `privilege: elevated` are not preserved, and the report states it.

## Services

`services` lists services with their state and start type. `state` narrows the list and `scope` selects system or user services. `start`, `restart`, `enable` and `disable` take services from the input, and `stop` ends services, processes and jobs.

```nurt
services state: running
services name: "nginx" |> restart
```

## Processes and ports

`processes` lists running processes, and `ports` lists ports with the processes that hold them. `open_files` names the processes that hold a file open, which explains `E_IN_USE`.

```nurt
processes name: "node" |> filter memory > 500mb |> select pid name memory
ports state: listen |> filter port == 8080
```

## Logs

`logs` reads events from the system log: the systemd journal, the Windows Event Log or the macOS unified log. `level` sets the lowest severity, `since` and `until` bound the time, and `message` filters the text.

```nurt
logs level: error since: ago(1h) limit: 50
```

## Packages and accounts

`package.list` and `package.search` read the package repositories, and `package.install`, `package.remove` and `package.upgrade` change installed packages through the manager of the system. `accounts` lists user accounts and groups, `host` describes the operating system and `environment` lists variables with the scope in which they are set. On Windows `windows.cim` queries CIM classes.

```nurt
package.list outdated: true
accounts kind: group
host
```

## Disks

`disks` lists mounted volumes with their capacity and free space. The `journal.space` command reports how much of that space the journal holds.

```nurt
disks |> filter free < 10gib
```

## Native administration commands

Every command below changes the system, accepts `privilege`, reports its effect and records the previous state in the journal. The inverse is the operation that `undo` runs. The commands are loaded with the group `administration` of the tool description, so a session that does not administer a system does not carry them.

| Group | Commands | Systems | Inverse |
|---|---|---|---|
| accounts | `accounts.create`, `accounts.modify` (shell, home, groups, comment, lock), `accounts.remove` (`keep_home: bool`), `accounts.password` | Linux, macOS, Windows | create and remove are inverse (the home directory is kept until the entry expires); `modify` restores the recorded values; `password` is irreversible |
| groups | `groups.create`, `groups.remove`, `groups.add_member`, `groups.remove_member` | Linux, macOS, Windows | pairwise |
| mounts | `mount` (device, target, type, options, `persistent`), `unmount` | Linux, macOS; Windows drive letters and folder mounts | `mount` and `unmount` |
| kernel | `sysctl.set` (key, value, `persistent`), `modules.load`, `modules.unload` | Linux; `sysctl` of writable keys on macOS | the previous value; load and unload |
| power | `power.restart`, `power.shutdown` (`at`, `delay`, `message`), `power.cancel` | all | irreversible once executed; a scheduled one is undone by `power.cancel` |
| disks | `disks.partition` (create, delete, resize), `disks.format` (file system, label) | Linux, macOS, Windows | irreversible |

## Network, clock and Windows management

The commands of the network, the clock, the services and the Windows management objects follow the same rules: they report their effect, record the previous state and accept `privilege`.

| Group | Commands | Systems | Inverse |
|---|---|---|---|
| firewall | `firewall.rules` (read), `firewall.allow`, `firewall.deny`, `firewall.remove` (port, protocol, source, direction, zone) | nftables, firewalld and ufw on Linux, pf on macOS, Windows Defender Firewall | the added rule is removed |
| network | `network.route_add`, `network.route_remove`, `network.dns_set` (servers, search domains) | all | the previous routes and DNS |
| clock | `clock.timezone_set`, `clock.set`, `clock.ntp` (on, off) | all | the previous time zone and NTP state; `clock.set` is irreversible |
| services | `start`, `stop`, `restart`, `enable`, `disable` | all | as in the table above |
| Windows management | `windows.cim` method calls (`invoke: <method>`) | Windows | irreversible unless the method has a documented opposite |

## Persistence and previews

A password is given as a secret reference of the engine and never as text; the journal does not store it. `mount` with `persistent: true` writes `/etc/fstab` or a systemd mount unit, and `sysctl.set` with `persistent: true` writes `/etc/sysctl.d/90-nurt.conf`; both files are journaled like any file, so `undo` restores them. The preview of `disks.partition` and `disks.format` lists the device, its partitions, file systems and mount points, and the size of the data that would be lost.

```nurt
accounts.create "deploy" shell: "/bin/bash" groups: ["www-data"] privilege: elevated
groups.add_member "www-data" "backup" privilege: elevated
```

## Several changes as one operation

A change of a system rarely is one command. `steps` runs several changing pipelines as one journal entry, all or nothing; a step marked irreversible (a restart, a program run with `run`, `power.restart`) is listed before the start and, after a later failure, is reported as not rolled back.

```nurt
steps {
    sysctl.set "net.ipv4.ip_forward" "1" persistent privilege: elevated
    firewall.allow port: 8443 protocol: tcp privilege: elevated
    let r = run ["systemctl", "reload", "app"] cwd: "/" privilege: elevated
    assert r.exit_code == 0
}
```

`when` chooses a branch by the state of the system, and `each` repeats a change over a list; `preview` shows the chosen branch and every iteration without a change. The syntax is described in [language](../site/language.md).

title: bash-migration
text:
# bash-migration

## What is corrected

A line that starts with a bash command is read with the rules of the POSIX shell and translated to a Nurt program. The result shows `corrected` and `ran`, the program that was executed. A translation that rests on an assumption and touches the target of a change is not applied: the answer is E_AMBIGUOUS with ready programs.

A line is a bash command when its first word is a bash command and it shows notation that only the shell has: a flag such as `-rf`, an operator such as `&&` or `>`, a quoted `'text'`, `$NAME`, an assignment before the program (`CI=1 npm test`) or an unquoted pattern. A first word that Nurt does not know at all (`touch`, `gzip`, `sha256sum`) needs none of these, and a word that Nurt reads as a synonym (`cat`, `ps`, `which`) is a bash command when its argument is a bare word that Nurt cannot take (`ps aux`, `which git`). A line with Nurt notation, a pipe `|>` or a named argument such as `glob:`, is always a Nurt program.

```text
rm -rf /srv/app/build
```

The line is corrected to `remove "/srv/app/build"`. The form to write directly uses a pattern, and the console lists the targets it computed:

```nurt
find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.tmp" |> remove
```

## Commands and flags

`mv A B` becomes `move "A" to: "B"`, `cp -r A B` becomes `copy "A" to: "B"`, `mkdir -p D` becomes `create "D" type: directory`, `touch F` becomes `create "F" type: file on_exists: touch`, `cat F` becomes `read "F"`, and `ls D` becomes `list "D"`. Recursion and the creation of missing parents are the default, so `-r` and `-p` need no counterpart.

A long flag or a short flag becomes the named parameter of the command with the same meaning: `grep -i` becomes `case_sensitive: false`, `grep -v` becomes `invert: true`, `grep -l` becomes `output: files`. A flag without a counterpart is an error that lists the parameters of the command.

## Privilege elevation

`sudo CMD`, `doas CMD` and `run0 CMD` become the translation of `CMD` with the call parameter `privilege: elevated`, and `sudo -u NAME CMD` (also `--user NAME`, `--user=NAME`) becomes the translation of `CMD` with `as_user: "NAME"`. The options `-n`, `-H`, `-E`, `-k`, `-b` and `--` are dropped. `sudo systemctl restart nginx` becomes `services name: "nginx" |> restart` with `privilege: elevated`; `sudo PROGRAM ARGS` where `PROGRAM` has no counterpart becomes `run ["PROGRAM", ARGS...] cwd: "..."` with `privilege: elevated`. `sudo -i`, `sudo -s`, `su` and `su -` open an elevated session, which is not a command: they end with `E_AMBIGUOUS` and a next step that gives the command with `privilege: elevated`. A group (`sudo -g`) and other options without a counterpart are reported with the option. The correction `run ["sudo", ...]` written in Nurt is replaced by the same `run` without `sudo` and with `privilege: elevated`.

## Redirection and variables

`echo "x" > F` becomes `write "F" "x\n" mode: overwrite` and `>>` becomes `mode: append`. A here-document written to a file becomes `write` with a raw text.

`$NAME` becomes `@NAME` when the program has a matching `let`. Inside a text the substitution is not translated: write `@name.path` as an argument instead.

```nurt
let files = find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.go"
run ["wc", "-l", ...@files.path] cwd: "/srv/app"
```

## Pipes, lists and sequences

A pipe `A | B` becomes `A |> B` when both sides translate. `find D -name P -delete` becomes `find "D" glob: "**/P" |> remove`. `xargs` and `find -exec` become a changing stage after `find`, or a `run` that receives `...@files.path`.

A list `A && B && C` or `A ; B` with several changing commands becomes one `steps` block: the steps run in order, the block is one journal entry, and a failure in any step rolls back the earlier ones (a `run` step is listed as not reversible). In a single call, the answer is `E_ONE_EFFECT`; `candidates` has the `steps` block as the first program and `next_steps` has the separate calls.

```text
mkdir -p /srv/out && cp -a /srv/in/data.csv /srv/out/
```

```nurt
steps {
    create "/srv/out" type: directory
    copy "/srv/in/data.csv" into: "/srv/out"
}
```

A list with one changing command stays that command. `cd D && make && make install` becomes a `steps` block of two `run` steps with `cwd: "D"`.

## Conditions

`if`, `elif` and `else` become `when`, `otherwise when` and `otherwise`. The tests `[ … ]`, `[[ … ]]` and `test` become a `bool` expression: `-e`, `-f`, `-d`, `-L`, `-s` (file tests, checked with `exists` and `info`), `-z`, `-n`, `=`, `==`, `!=`, `=~` (a regular expression), `-eq`, `-ne`, `-gt`, `-ge`, `-lt`, `-le`, with `!`, `-a`, `-o`, `&&` and `||` as `not`, `and` and `or`. A command used as a condition (`if systemctl is-active x`) has a translation only when it is a `run`; its exit code is `r.exit_code == 0` after `let r = run …`.

```text
if [ -f /srv/a ]; then rm /srv/a; fi
```

```nurt
when exists("/srv/a") and ((info "/srv/a" |> first 1)).type == "file" {
    remove "/srv/a" on_missing: error
}
```

`case` becomes the same chain: every pattern is `==` for a literal and `~` for a pattern with `*`, `?` or `[…]`, `a|b)` is `or`, `*)` is `otherwise`.

`test -f F || CMD` and `[ … ] || CMD` become `when not (…) { CMD }`. `CMD || true` is `CMD` with the assumption that its failure is no longer ignored. Any other `A || B` has no translation: the error lists `A` and `B` as separate programs. `[ … ] && CMD` is `when … { CMD }`.

## Loops

`for x in PATTERN; do … done` becomes `each (find … ) as x { … }`: the variable is a record and `$x` becomes `@x.path`. `for x in $(CMD)` is `each (CMD) as x` when `CMD` reads records. `for x in a b c` is `each ["a", "b", "c"] as x`. `for x in "$@"` is `each @args as x` with the script parameter `args`. `while [ … ]; do … done` becomes `while … { … }`, and `until [ … ]; do …; sleep N; done` becomes `repeat until: … every: Ns { … }` (the body runs once before the first test, which the translation reports as an assumption). `break` and `continue` stay as they are.

Not translated: the arithmetic `for ((…))`, `select`, a loop body that uses `$x` inside a longer text (write `@x.path`), and a pipe into `while read`.

## Functions and script parameters

`f() { … }` and `function f { … }` become `define f(…) { … }`. A parameter is named after the variable that takes `$1`, `$2` (`dir="$1"`, `days=${2:-30}`), and is `arg1`, `arg2` otherwise, with a note in the report. A call `f x y` becomes `f("x", "y")`.

In a script, `$1`, `$2` and `$@` outside functions become the `params` block that starts the program, the type is taken from the use (`path` for the operand of `rm`, `cp` and the file tests, `int` for `-eq`, `-gt` and the other numeric tests, `text` otherwise), a default `${2:-30}` is the default of the parameter, `shift` moves the numbering, `$@` is the list `args`, and `getopts` declares one parameter per option: `bool` for a flag, `text` for an option with an argument. The program is called with `nurt run script.nurt dir: "/srv" days: 7`.

```text
dir="$1"
keep=${2:-7}
rm -rf "$dir"
```

```nurt
params {
    dir: path
    keep: text = "7"
}
remove @dir
```

## Administration of accounts, mounts and the kernel

| Bash | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `mkfifo [-m MODE] P` | `create "P" type: fifo mode: "MODE"` |
| `mknod P p`, `mknod P c|b MAJOR MINOR` | `create "P" type: fifo`, `create "P" type: device kind: char|block major: MAJOR minor: MINOR` |
| `useradd [-m] [-s SHELL] [-d HOME] [-G G1,G2] [-c TEXT] [-u UID] [-r] NAME` | `accounts.create name: "NAME" …` |
| `usermod [-s] [-d] [-G] [-c] [-L or -U] NAME` | `accounts.modify name: "NAME" …` (`-L` is `lock: true`, `-U` is `lock: false`) |
| `usermod -aG GROUP NAME` | `groups.add_member name: "GROUP" member: "NAME"` |
| `userdel [-r] NAME` | `accounts.remove name: "NAME" keep_home: true`; with `-r`, `keep_home: false` |
| `groupadd [-g GID] [-r] NAME`, `groupdel NAME` | `groups.create name: "NAME" …`, `groups.remove name: "NAME"` |
| `gpasswd -a USER GROUP`, `gpasswd -d USER GROUP` | `groups.add_member`, `groups.remove_member` |
| `passwd NAME` | `accounts.password name: "NAME"`; the password comes from a secret reference of the engine, never from the program |
| `mount [-t T] [-o O1,O2] DEVICE TARGET`, `umount TARGET` | `mount device: "DEVICE" target: "TARGET" type: "T" options: ["O1", "O2"]`, `unmount target: "TARGET"` |
| `sysctl -w KEY=VALUE` (one key per call) | `sysctl.set key: "KEY" value: "VALUE"` |

## Modules and firewall

| Bash | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `modprobe MODULE [PARAM…]`, `modprobe -r MODULE`, `rmmod MODULE` | `modules.load name: "MODULE" params: […]`, `modules.unload name: "MODULE"` |
| `ufw allow or deny PORT[/PROTO]`, `ufw allow from SOURCE to any port PORT proto PROTO` | `firewall.allow` or `firewall.deny` with `port: PORT protocol: "PROTO" source: "SOURCE"` |
| `firewall-cmd [--zone=Z] --add-port=PORT/PROTO`, `--remove-port=…` | `firewall.allow port: PORT protocol: "PROTO" zone: "Z"`, `firewall.remove …` |
| `nft add rule … input or output tcp or udp dport PORT accept or drop`, `iptables -A INPUT or OUTPUT -p tcp or udp --dport PORT -j ACCEPT or DROP [-s SOURCE]` | `firewall.allow` or `firewall.deny` with `port: PORT protocol: "tcp" direction: "in"` or `"out"` |

## Routes, name servers, clock, power and disks

| Bash | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `ip route add DEST via GW dev IF metric N`, `ip route del DEST` | `network.route_add destination: "DEST" gateway: "GW" interface: "IF" metric: N`, `network.route_remove destination: "DEST"` |
| `resolvectl dns IF SERVER…` | `network.dns_set interface: "IF" servers: ["SERVER", …]` |
| `timedatectl set-timezone ZONE`, `date -s "TIME"` | `clock.timezone_set "ZONE"`, `clock.set "TIME"` |
| `shutdown -r or -h [now or +MINUTES] [MESSAGE]`, `shutdown -c`, `reboot`, `poweroff`, `halt` | `power.restart` or `power.shutdown` with `delay: Nm` and `message: "…"`, `power.cancel`, `power.restart`, `power.shutdown` |
| `parted -s DEVICE rm N`, `parted -s DEVICE mkpart … START END` | `disks.partition device: "DEVICE" action: "delete" number: N`, `action: "create" start: "START" end: "END"` |
| `mkfs.FS [-L LABEL] DEVICE`, `mkfs -t FS DEVICE` | `disks.format device: "DEVICE" fs: "FS" label: "LABEL"` |
| `sqlite3 DB "SQL"` | `sql "DB" "SQL"` |

A rule beyond a port rule (`iptables -t nat …`, a rule with a match module) is run with `run ["iptables", …] cwd: "/"`, and with `privilege: elevated` when written with `sudo`. A form with an option that has no counterpart is an error that names the option. `sudo` before any of these commands adds `privilege: elevated`, as for every command.

## What is rejected

Only forms that depend on the shell itself have no translation: `eval`, subshells `( … )` and groups `{ …; }`, the arithmetic `for ((…))`, `select`, interactive input (`read`) and here-documents other than `cat > file`. `cd D && CMD` is translated only for an absolute path in the same line, as the `cwd` of `run` or as paths resolved against `D`; other uses of `cd` are rejected with a note on the call parameter `base`. A script that needs one of them runs unchanged with `run ["bash", "script.sh"] cwd: "/srv/app"`.

## Scripts

An existing shell script is run unchanged through `run ["bash", "script.sh"] cwd: "/srv/app"`. The command `nurt migrate` translates a script to a Nurt program with conditions, loops, functions and `params`, and reports what it could not translate. A function defined in the script is a `define`, and the later calls of it are calls.

title: documents
text:
# documents

## Key paths

A key addresses a value inside a document. The forms are `a.b` for a map entry, `a[0].b` for a list item, `a[*]` for every item of a list, `a.**` for all descendants, `a["dotted.key"]` for a key that contains a dot, `a[?name == "x"]` for the items that meet a condition and `a[+]` for a new item at the end of a list.

## Reading

`read` with `key` returns the value at a key path. `query` applies a jq filter to a document, a file or a response and returns items that later stages can filter and select.

```nurt
read "/srv/app/values.yaml" key: "image.tag"
query ".dependencies | keys" path: "/srv/app/package.json"
```

## Changing

`set` writes a value at a key path and keeps the layout, comments, key order and style of the file; only the bytes of the changed value change. The format is detected from the file and can be given with `format`. `create: true` adds a missing key, and `values` sets several keys in one call.

```nurt
set "/srv/app/package.json" key: "scripts.test" value: "vitest"
```

## Validation

A write that introduces a new syntax error into a known format is rolled back. `validate: warn` reports the error and keeps the change, and `validate: off` skips the check. The supported formats are `json`, `jsonc`, `yaml`, `toml`, `xml`, `ini`, `csv`, `tsv`, `properties`, `env` and `plist`. A change to a file that was modified after it was read fails with `E_STALE`; see the guide `multi-agent`.

## Databases

`sql` runs statements on an SQLite database file. A call whose statements only read opens the database read-only. A statement that changes anything opens it for writing, and the change is recorded in the journal like any other change: the database file and its `-wal`, `-shm` and `-journal` files are preserved first, and `undo` restores them. `write: true` is optional; `write: false` keeps the call read-only. `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and `END` merge with the transaction of the call, `ROLLBACK` ends it with `E_ROLLED_BACK`, and `ATTACH`, `VACUUM INTO`, `VACUUM`, `load_extension` and the pragmas `temp_store_directory` and `data_store_directory` are allowed (see the command page).

```nurt
sql "/srv/app/app.db" "select id, name from users where active = 1 limit 5"
```

## Errors

`E_KEY_NOT_FOUND` names a key that does not exist and lists the keys at the nearest level. `E_KEY_SYNTAX` marks a malformed key path. `E_DOC_PARSE` means the file is not valid in its format, and `E_FORMAT` means the format could not be determined.

title: encodings
text:
# encodings

## Detection

Text files are read in the encoding that Nurt detects: a byte order mark, valid UTF-8 or a code page. The `entry` record of `info` and `find` has the fields `encoding`, `line_ending` and `binary`, so a set of files can be inspected before any change.

```nurt
find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.txt" |> select path encoding line_ending
```

## Preservation

A change to a text file keeps its encoding, its line endings and its byte order mark. Output of commands is always UTF-8. `read` with `encoding` forces the encoding when the detection is wrong, and `write` with `encoding`, `line_ending` and `bom` sets them for a new file.

```nurt
read "/srv/legacy/readme.txt" encoding: "windows-1250"
write "/srv/app/notes.txt" "first\nsecond\n" line_ending: crlf bom: true
```

## Conversion

`convert` changes the encoding, the line endings or the byte order mark of files. A parameter that is not given leaves that property unchanged, and `line_ending: keep` states this explicitly. The conversion is recorded in the journal and can be undone.

```nurt
convert "/srv/legacy/readme.txt" encoding: "utf-8" line_ending: lf
find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.txt" |> filter line_ending == "crlf" |> convert line_ending: lf
```

## Mixed and invalid content

A file that mixes line endings keeps each line ending unless `convert` is applied. A byte sequence that is not valid in the encoding fails with `E_ENCODING` and the position of the first invalid byte. A file that contains binary data is skipped by `search` and `replace` unless `binary: text` is given.

## Errors

`E_ENCODING` reports an invalid sequence or an unsupported encoding name. `E_BINARY` reports that a text command met binary content. `E_UNSUPPORTED` reports an encoding that Nurt does not convert.

title: git-workflow
text:
# git-workflow

## Built-in operations

All operations of the group `git` are built in and work without an installed git: status, diff, log, show, blame, branch, stage, commit, tag, fetch, clone, switch, restore, reset, merge, rebase, stash, pull, push, worktree and checkpoint. `fetch`, `clone`, `pull` and `push` act outside the local file system and are recorded as irreversible. Authentication failures are reported as `E_GIT_AUTH` and unknown SSH hosts as `E_GIT_HOST_KEY`.

```nurt
git.status "/srv/app"
git.log "/srv/app" count: 5 path: ["/srv/app/a.go"]
```

## Reviewing before a commit

`git.diff` shows differences between revisions, the index and the working tree, with `staged`, `stat` and `symbol` narrowing the result. `git.review` checks changes before a commit for conflict markers, whitespace errors, large or binary files, secrets, missing tests and the format of the subject.

```nurt
git.diff "/srv/app" staged: true stat: true
git.review "/srv/app" scope: staged checks: ["conflict_markers", "secrets"]
```

## Committing

`git.stage` stages files, hunks or lines, and `git.commit` records a commit with `message`, `paths` or `all`, and optional `trailers` and `sign_off`. A commit hook that fails stops the commit with `E_GIT_HOOK`. An empty commit fails with `E_GIT_NOTHING_TO_COMMIT` unless `allow_empty` is set.

```nurt
git.commit "/srv/app" message: "fix: parser" paths: ["/srv/app/a.go"]
```

## Checkpoints and undo

`git.checkpoint` keeps a snapshot of the working tree and index outside the branches, and `action: restore` returns to it. Operations that change local state, such as commit, switch, merge, rebase, reset and stash, are recorded in the journal; `undo` reverts a commit or a merge by moving the branch back to its previous revision.

```nurt
git.checkpoint "/srv/app" action: create label: "before-refactoring"
git.checkpoint "/srv/app" action: restore label: "before-refactoring"
```

## Branches and remotes

`git.branch` lists, creates, renames and deletes branches, and `git.switch` changes the working tree to a branch. A switch with local changes that would be overwritten fails with `E_GIT_DIRTY`. `git.push` with `force: lease` refuses to overwrite commits that were not fetched, and a push that the remote rejects fails with `E_GIT_PUSH_REJECTED`.

```nurt
git.switch "/srv/app" branch: "feature/parser" create: true
git.push "/srv/app" remote: "origin" branch: "feature/parser" set_upstream: true
```

title: journal-undo
text:
# journal-undo

## The journal

Every change to files, provider values or repository state is recorded with the previous state. `history` lists the operations, newest first, with their state: `available`, `partial`, `expired` or `undone`. `limit`, `since`, `before` and `path` narrow the list.

```nurt
history limit: 10
history path: "/srv/app/main.go"
```

## Undoing and redoing

`undo` reverts the last operation, or the operation named by `id`. `to` and `since` revert several operations, newest first, and `paths` restores only the named paths of an operation. `redo` applies an undone operation again. Undo repairs a mistake that is visible in the result; checking with `preview: true` or `assert` before the change is still the safer course.

```nurt
undo paths: ["/srv/app/main.go"]
redo
```

## Conflicts

When a file changed after the operation, undoing it would discard the later change. `on_conflict` selects the behavior: `report` stops and lists the conflicts, `abort` leaves everything as it was, `force` restores the old state, `include_later` also reverts the later operations and `partial` restores the paths without a conflict. The error `E_JOURNAL_CONFLICT` lists the conflicting paths.

```nurt
undo on_conflict: partial
```

## Partial and irreversible entries

An entry is `partial` when the previous state of some targets could not be kept. `history state: partial` lists such entries, and `undo on_conflict: partial` restores what was kept. Effects outside the file system, such as the start of a service or a push to a remote, are recorded as irreversible and are reported separately. The error `E_JOURNAL_PARTIAL` marks an undo that restored only part of an operation.

## Limits and space

Entries expire when the limits of the journal are exceeded. `journal.status` shows the number of entries, the space used, the oldest entry and the active limits. `journal.limits` shows or changes the limits, `journal.pin` protects entries from expiry and `journal.space` reports the space that the journal holds on each volume. `journal.purge` releases entries and the space they hold, and cannot be undone.

```nurt
journal.status
journal.limits scope: user
journal.space
```

title: large-results
text:
# large-results

## Paging

A result is limited by the call parameter `limit`, 50 records by default, and the answer carries a `cursor` that continues the result in the next call. The program is the same in each call; only `cursor` changes. A limit keeps the answer within the budget of the caller without changing the effect of the program.

## Continuing a shortened result

A response that leaves lines, records or the end of long lines out carries the field `continuation` and ends with the hint "more: next". The call `next` returns the next part, in the same record type as the first response, until `remaining` is 0; the program does not run again and the parts are consistent with the first response.

```nurt
next
next 200
next c3 200
next all
next full
```

`next c3` continues the continuation `c3` when several results are open, `next 200` reads 200 units, `next all` everything that is left and `next full` the lines of the last part that were cut, whole. The part is a result like any other: `next |> filter severity == "error"`. Kept results expire after `continuation.max_age` (1 hour), and the limits `continuation.max_count` (50) and `continuation.max_size` (256 MiB) remove the oldest first; an expired continuation ends with `E_CONTINUATION_EXPIRED` and the original call in `next_steps`.

## Fewer fields

The call parameter `fields` lists the fields of each record to return. `select` does the same inside a program and also adds computed fields, so later stages and the result carry only the fields that are needed.

```nurt
find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.go" |> select path size
find "/srv/app" glob: "**/*.go" |> select path total: size * 2
```

## Counting and summarizing

`count` returns the number of records and `summarize` computes count, sum, minimum, maximum and average of fields, optionally per group with `by`. `group` counts the records of each value of a field. These stages answer a question about a large set without returning the set.

```nurt
find "/srv/app" |> count
find "/srv/app" |> summarize size by: type
search "deprecated" "/srv/app/src" |> group path
```

## Narrowing early

A condition placed close to the source reduces the data that later stages process. `first` with `sort` returns the largest or newest entries, and `search` with `output: counts` or `output: files` returns counts or file names instead of lines.

```nurt
find "/srv/app" |> sort size order: desc |> first 10
search "deprecated" "/srv/app/src" output: counts
```

## Saved output

The call parameter `save_to` writes the full result to a file and returns a summary with the path of the file. A program that writes a lot of output can limit what returns with `show: errors` or `show: summary`, and `head` and `tail` keep the first or last lines.

```nurt
run ["make", "all"] cwd: "/srv/app" show: errors tail: 40
```

title: multi-agent
text:
# multi-agent

## The etag

Every file read carries an `etag`, a value that identifies its content. A change to the file is applied only when the file still has the content that was read. `read` and `info` return the `etag` in their records, and a changing command checks it before it writes.

```nurt
info "/srv/app/config.toml"
```

## Conditional writes

The parameter `if_match` makes the check explicit: the change is applied only when the file has the given `etag`. `write`, `replace`, `insert`, `edit`, `set` and `patch` accept it. Without `if_match` the check uses the state that the same call read.

```nurt
write "/srv/app/config.toml" "mode = 1\n" if_match: "a41f9c"
```

## Stale content

A change to a file that another session modified after it was read fails with `E_STALE` and leaves the file unchanged. The error names the path and the current `etag`. The remedy is to read the file again, decide whether the change still applies and send the change with the new `etag`.

## Retrying

A read that follows `E_STALE` returns the current content. `read` with `unchanged_since` returns nothing when the file did not change since the given `etag`, which makes a repeated check cheap. A program that changes several files stops at the first conflict before any file is written.

```nurt
read "/srv/app/config.toml" unchanged_since: "a41f9c"
```

## Sessions and the journal

The call parameter `session` names the session of a call. The journal records the session of each operation, and `history` lists the operations of all sessions; `undo` reverts only the operations of the current session unless `all_sessions: true` is given. An undo of an operation whose files were changed by another session reports the conflict instead of discarding the other change; see the guide `journal-undo`.

```nurt
history limit: 20
```

title: notebooks
text:
# notebooks

## Cells

A notebook is a list of cells with a type, a source and outputs. `notebook.cells` lists them. `view: outline` returns one line per cell, `outputs` selects whether outputs are omitted, summarized, returned as text or returned in full, and `find` returns only cells that contain a text.

```nurt
notebook.cells "/srv/a.ipynb" view: outline
notebook.cells "/srv/a.ipynb" find: "import pandas" scope: source
```

## Index and identifier

A cell is addressed by `index`, its position, or by `id`, its identifier. A position changes when cells are inserted or removed; an identifier does not. Notebooks written by older tools can lack identifiers: `notebook.normalize` adds them and the missing fields of the format.

```nurt
notebook.normalize "/srv/a.ipynb"
```

## Changing cells

`notebook.replace` replaces the source or the type of a cell, or text inside cell sources with `find` and `with`. `notebook.insert` adds a cell at a position or after the cell named by `after_id`. `notebook.move`, `notebook.copy` and `notebook.remove` change the order and the set of cells.

```nurt
notebook.replace "/srv/a.ipynb" index: 3 source: "print(1)"
notebook.insert "/srv/a.ipynb" after_id: "c3" cell_type: markdown source: "## Results"
```

## Outputs and several changes

`notebook.clear_outputs` removes the outputs of cells, and `reset_outputs` of `notebook.replace` does the same for the cells it changes. `notebook.ops` applies a list of cell operations in one write, so the notebook is never left half changed.

```nurt
notebook.clear_outputs "/srv/a.ipynb"
```

## Export

`notebook.export` writes a notebook to a new file as a script, Markdown or text with `format`. The notebook itself is not changed. Outputs are not part of an exported script.

```nurt
notebook.export "/srv/a.ipynb" to: "/srv/a.py" format: script
```

title: powershell-migration
text:
# powershell-migration

## What is corrected

A line that starts with a cmdlet in the form `Verb-Noun`, or with an alias of one, and whose arguments have the form `-Parameter value` is translated to a Nurt program. Every translated cmdlet has a table of parameters; a parameter without a counterpart is an error that lists the parameters of the Nurt command. The result shows `corrected` and `ran`.

## Files and text

`Get-ChildItem -Path D` becomes `list "D"`. With `-Recurse -Filter "*.go"` it becomes `find "D" glob: "**/*.go"`. `Get-Content F -Tail N` becomes `read "F" last: N`. `Set-Content`, `Add-Content` and `Out-File` become `write` with `mode: overwrite` or `mode: append`. `Select-String` ignores case by default, so the translation adds `case_sensitive: false`.

`Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Remove-Item`, `Rename-Item` and `New-Item` become `copy`, `move`, `remove`, `rename` and `create`. `Test-Path P` becomes `info "P"`, whose record has the field `exists`.

```nurt
find "/home/user/app" glob: "**/*.go" |> filter size > 1mb |> sort size order: desc |> first 5
```

## Filtering objects

`Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB }` becomes `filter size > 1mb`. Only comparisons of fields, `-and`, `-or` and `-not` are translated, with the fields `Length`, `LastWriteTime`, `Name`, `FullName` and `Extension` mapped to `size`, `modified`, `name`, `path` and `extension`.

`ForEach-Object { … }` has no counterpart. The exceptions are blocks that read one property, such as `{ $_.Name }`, which become `select name`. A loop over records that change something is written with `each` (see below); a computed value is written as `select total: size * 2`.

`Group-Object` and `Measure-Object` become `group by:` and `summarize`. `X | Get-Member` becomes `X |> describe`.

## Registry, services and processes

A registry path such as `HKLM:\Software\X` becomes the path `"registry:/HKLM/Software/X"` and works in `list`, `read` and `write`. `Get-Service`, `Start-Service` and `Stop-Service` become `services name: "N"` followed by `|> start` or `|> stop`. `Get-Process` and `Stop-Process` become `processes` and `|> stop`.

## Elevation

`Start-Process -Verb RunAs`, `sudo`-like wrappers and running the console as the administrator have no text translation. Give the call parameter `privilege: elevated` (or `as_user` on Linux and macOS) on the stage that needs the rights; on Windows the backend `self` runs in the same process when the console is elevated, and the service backend arrives in 0.1.2.

## Common parameters

`-WhatIf` becomes the call parameter `preview: true`. `-Confirm` is removed with a note, because Nurt does not ask for confirmation. `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` becomes `on_missing: skip` where the command has the parameter.

## Conditions, loops, functions and parameters

The corrections translate single cmdlets. The constructs of a script are written in Nurt by hand, because they are part of the language and not of the correction of one line. Each construct is one journal entry and all or nothing, which `try`/`catch` and `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` do not give.

| PowerShell | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `if (…) { … } elseif (…) { … } else { … }` | `when … { … } otherwise when … { … } otherwise { … }` |
| `Test-Path P` in a condition | `exists "P"` |
| `foreach ($f in Get-ChildItem …) { … }`, `… \| ForEach-Object { … }` with a change | `each (find …) as f { … }`; the record is `f`, a field is `f.path` |
| `while (…) { … }` | `while … limit: 20 { … }` |
| `do { … } until (…)` | `repeat until: … every: 5s limit: 2m { … }` |
| `break`, `continue` | `break`, `continue` inside a loop |
| `A; B; C` with changes that must stand or fall together | `steps { A  B  C }` |

## Script parameters

A script declares its parameters with `params`; `-WhatIf` becomes `preview`, as in this example.

| PowerShell | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `function F($Dir, $Keep = 7) { … }` | `define F(dir: path, keep: int = 7) { … }`; a call is `F("/x", keep: 14)` |
| `param([string]$Dir, [int]$Days = 30, [switch]$Dry)` | `params { dir: path  days: int = 30  dry: bool = false }`; a switch is a `bool` written without a value (`dry`) |
| `$LASTEXITCODE`, `$?` | `exit_code` and the fields of a `let` bound to `run` |

```nurt
params {
    dir: path
    days: int = 30
    dry: bool = false
}
find @dir glob: "**/*.log" |> filter modified < ago(@days * 1d) |> remove preview: @dry
```

`nurt run cleanup.nurt dir: "D:/logs" days: 7 dry` passes the values, as `.\cleanup.ps1 -Dir D:\logs -Days 7 -Dry` does. `-WhatIf` of a script is the parameter `preview` of every stage.

## Administration

The native commands of the administration group replace the modules of the system. The full list, the systems and the inverse operation of each command are in [administration](administration.md).

| PowerShell | Nurt |
|---|---|
| `New-LocalUser`, `Set-LocalUser`, `Remove-LocalUser` | `accounts.create`, `accounts.modify`, `accounts.remove` |
| `New-LocalGroup`, `Add-LocalGroupMember`, `Remove-LocalGroupMember` | `groups.create`, `groups.add_member`, `groups.remove_member` |
| `New-NetFirewallRule`, `Remove-NetFirewallRule` | `firewall.allow` or `firewall.deny`, `firewall.remove` |
| `Set-DnsClientServerAddress`, `New-NetRoute` | `network.dns_set`, `network.route_add` |
| `Set-TimeZone`, `Set-Date` | `clock.timezone_set`, `clock.set` |
| `Restart-Computer`, `Stop-Computer` | `power.restart`, `power.shutdown` |
| `New-Partition`, `Format-Volume` | `disks.partition`, `disks.format` |
| `Invoke-CimMethod` | `windows.cim` with `invoke: <method>` |

## What is rejected

`Invoke-Expression` is rejected: Nurt has no `eval`. `Set-Location` and `Push-Location` are rejected with an explanation of the call parameter `base` and the parameter `cwd` of `run`. Output cmdlets such as `Write-Output X` become `evaluate "X"` and `Get-Date` becomes `evaluate now()`.

title: refactoring
text:
# refactoring

## Text, syntax and symbols

`search` and `replace` work on text. `search mode: syntax` matches syntax patterns, so a match inside a comment or a string is not confused with code, and `scope: code` limits a text search to code. The `code.*` commands work on symbols: a symbol has a definition and references that a text search cannot tell apart from other uses of the same word.

## Finding symbols

`code.symbols` finds definitions by name across a repository. `kind` narrows the result to functions, methods, classes and other symbol kinds, and `match` selects exact, prefix, substring, fuzzy or regular expression comparison. `code.outline` lists the symbols of one file, and `code.references` lists the places that use a symbol.

```nurt
code.symbols "oldName" path: ["/srv/app/src"] kind: function
code.references "/srv/app/src/a.go" line: 12 column: 6
```

## Renaming

`code.rename` renames a symbol and its references in all files as one operation, so a single `undo` reverts it. The symbol comes from the input or from the arguments `path`, `line` and `column`. The parameter `source` selects the analysis: `lsp` uses an installed language server, `syntax` uses the local syntax analysis, and `auto` chooses the first that is available.

```nurt
code.symbols "oldName" path: ["/srv/app/src"] kind: function |> code.rename "newName"
```

## Checking after a change

A rename that compiles is not proof that the behavior is unchanged. `verify` runs a check after the change and rolls the change back when the check fails. `code.diagnostics` reports errors and warnings in changed files.

```nurt
code.rename "newName" path: "/srv/app/src/a.go" line: 12 column: 6 |> verify (run ["go", "build", "./..."] cwd: "/srv/app" |> assert exit_code: 0)
```

## Limits

A text replacement of a name changes every occurrence, including unrelated ones. When a text replacement is the only option, `check_references` reports references that would remain unchanged, and `assert paths: N` stops the program when the number of affected files differs from the expected one. Dynamic uses of a name, such as names built from strings, are not references and are not renamed.

title: running-programs
text:
# running-programs

## Starting a program

`run` starts a program without a shell. The first argument is a list: the program followed by its arguments, so no quoting rules of a shell apply. `cwd` sets the working directory, `env` adds variables and `inherit_env: none` starts the program with an empty environment. A program that does not exist fails with `E_PROGRAM_NOT_FOUND`.

```nurt
run ["go", "test", "./..."] cwd: "/srv/app" |> assert exit_code: 0
```

## Waiting, limits and background jobs

By default `run` waits for the program. `timeout` stops a program that runs longer, and `idle_timeout` stops a program that writes nothing for the given time. With `background: true` the call returns a job at once, and `jobs` reads its state, output or result later. `stop` ends a job and `retry` runs it again with the same directory and environment.

```nurt
run ["make", "all"] cwd: "/srv/app" background: true
jobs state: running
```

## Output

`show` selects what the result contains: `stdout`, `stderr`, `both`, `errors`, `summary` or `none`. `head` and `tail` keep the first or last lines, `filter` keeps the lines that match a pattern and `dedupe` (on by default) collapses repeated lines, also lines that differ only in numbers.
