already expired. With the common parameter `preview: true` the command
reports the effective limits and the entries that would expire, and changes
nothing.

`scope: session` keeps the limits until the session of the request ends, or
until `session.ttl` passes without calls of the session. `scope: user` writes
the `[journal]` section of the user configuration file, or the
`[journal.volume."<mount>"]` table with `volume`, keeping its comments and
layout. Missing directories of the file are created. The change is recorded
as a journal entry of kind `journal.limits` that does not count as a step;
`undo` of that entry restores the previous content of the file. `scope: user`
requires the location of the user configuration file to be configured for
the journal; otherwise a call that sets a limit fails with `E_UNSUPPORTED`,
and a call without `steps`, `age` and `size` only reports.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `steps` | `int \| enum(unlimited)` | none | Maximum number of entries kept. |
| `age` | `duration \| enum(unlimited)` | none | Maximum age of entries kept. |
| `size` | `size \| percent \| enum(unlimited)` | none | Maximum journal size as a size such as 20gib, a share of the volume such as "10%" or a share of free space such as "50%free". |
| `scope` | `enum(session\|user)` | `session` | Change the limits for this session or persistently for the account. |
| `volume` | `path` | none | Only the journal of the volume that contains this path. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `journal_state`, `effect` |

Without `steps`, `age` and `size` the output is one `journal_state` record per
selected volume, as from `journal.status`. Otherwise the output is one
`effect` record of kind `journal.limits`: `after.applied` states whether the
new limits were set, `after.expiring` lists the entries that expire (or would
expire with `preview`), `after.expiring_bytes` gives their logical size, and
`after.volumes` lists the effective limits of each selected volume with their
sources.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `journal` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| Reversibility conditions | Restoring the previous limits does not bring back entries that expired under the new limits; without parameters the command only reads. |

The limits are reversed by setting them again. Entries that expired under the
new limits cannot be restored; the result then carries the irreversible
marker `journal_entries_expired`. Without parameters the command only reads.

## Examples

Show the limits of every volume and the levels that set them:

```nurt example
journal.limits
```

Keep the last 10 operations for five minutes in this session:

```nurt example
journal.limits steps: 10 age: 5m
```

Keep the last 100 operations for one day in this session:

```nurt example
journal.limits steps: 100 age: 24h
```

Limit the journal on the volume of the project to a tenth of its capacity,
persistently for the account:

```nurt example
journal.limits size: "10%" scope: user volume: "/home/user/project"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | a value is out of its range, or `scope: session` is used by a request without a session | use a value within the range; set the request option `session` or use `scope: user` |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | no journal volume contains `volume` | omit `volume` or name a path on a volume with a journal |
| `E_CONFIG` | the user configuration file is not valid TOML or UTF-8 | correct the file, then repeat the call |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | `scope: user` and no user configuration file is configured for the journal | configure the location of the user configuration file or use `scope: session` |
| `E_IO` | a file of the journal or the configuration cannot be written | check the permissions of the state directory |

## Related

`journal.status`, `journal.purge`, `journal.pin`, `journal.space`.

title: journal.pin
text:
# journal.pin

## Synopsis

```text
journal.pin <id>... [name: value]...
```

## Description

`journal.pin` protects journal entries from expiry by the step limit, the age
limit and the size budget for the given duration. A pinned entry stays
undoable after newer operations, time and other entries would have expired
it. Pinning never protects an entry from reclaim when the volume needs space
for the user: free space for the user always has priority.

Without `until` the pin lasts `journal.pin_max_age` (24 hours by default).
Pinning a pinned entry again replaces its pin. `release: true` removes the
pins; released entries that are over a limit at that moment expire at once
and are listed in `expired`.

The pin is recorded outside the entry, in the journal directory of every
volume that holds a part of the operation. Pinning changes neither the entry
nor its hash, creates no journal entry and consumes no operation number and
no step.

Entries that do not exist, expired or were undone are listed in
`not_available` and left alone. The result does not state when a pin ends;
`history` shows whether an operation is pinned.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `list<int>` | none | Entries to pin or release. |
| `release` | `bool` | `false` | Release the pin instead of setting it. |
| `until` | `duration` | the configured maximum pin age | Duration of the pin. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `journal` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| Reversibility conditions | Pinned entries can still be released when the volume runs out of space. |

## Examples

Keep operation 18 undoable for the default duration:

```nurt example
journal.pin 18
```

Pin two operations for three days:

```nurt example
journal.pin 18 19 until: 3d
```

Release the pin of operation 18:

```nurt example
journal.pin 18 release: true
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_IO` | the pin file of a volume cannot be written, or the journal of a volume of the entry is not available | mount the volume and check its journal with `journal.status` |

## Related

`history`, `journal.status`, `journal.limits`, `journal.purge`, `undo`.

title: journal.purge
text:
# journal.purge

## Synopsis

```text
journal.purge [name: value]...
```

## Description

`journal.purge` releases journal entries at once, together with the space
their data holds. Without `up_to` and `id` every entry of the selected volumes
is released; `up_to` releases the entries up to and including that operation
number; `id` releases exactly the listed entries and keeps older ones.

Pinned entries are released as well: a pin protects an entry from expiry by
steps, age and size, not from an explicit release. An operation that spans
several volumes is released on all of them, so that no entry is left
partially undoable.

A released entry becomes `expired` with the reason `purge`; a tombstone with
its metrics remains for `history`. Committed, partial and undone entries are
released; entries that are already expired, being reclaimed or corrupt are not
changed. The release is recorded in the audit log of the account; it creates
no journal entry and consumes no step.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `volume` | `path \| enum(all)` | `all` | Volume whose journal is purged, or all volumes. |
| `up_to` | `int` | none | Release all entries up to and including this operation number. |
| `id` | `list<int>` | none | Release only these entries, keeping older ones. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

The `effect` record of kind `journal.purge` lists the numbers of the released
entries in `after.released` and their logical size in `after.bytes`;
`summary.released` counts them, and `irreversible` carries `purged` when at
least one entry was released.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `journal` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `irreversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Released entries can no longer be undone; the result carries the
irreversible marker `purged`.

## Examples

Release every entry of every volume:

```nurt example
journal.purge
```

Release the entries up to operation 120 on the volume of a project:

```nurt example
journal.purge volume: "/home/user/project" up_to: 120
```

Release two large entries and keep the rest:

```nurt example
journal.purge id: [131, 134]
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | no journal volume contains `volume` | omit `volume` or name a path on a volume with a journal |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | both `up_to` and `id` are given, or `id` lists no entry | give one of them |
| `E_IO` | a journal directory cannot be changed | check the permissions of the journal directory |

## Related

`journal.status`, `journal.limits`, `journal.pin`, `history`.

title: journal.space
text:
# journal.space

## Synopsis

```text
journal.space [name: value]...
```

## Description

Reports one `volume` record per journal volume: free space as other programs
see it, the space the journal holds and could release, and the thresholds that
protect user space. Without `volume` the command reports every volume known to
the space service; with `volume` it reports the volume that contains the path.

Free space `F` is the space available to the account after the journal took
its share and after the account quota, when quotas apply (`statvfs` on Linux,
`volumeAvailableCapacityKey` on macOS, `GetDiskFreeSpaceExW` on Windows).
Purgeable space reported by macOS is not counted.

The thresholds are derived from the capacity `T` of the volume, or from the
account quota when that is smaller:

| Threshold | Key | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Reserve `R` | `space.reserve` | 15 % of `T`, clamped to `space.reserve_min` (5 GiB) and `space.reserve_max` (50 GiB); with an account quota no more than 15 % of the quota |
| Soft threshold `S` | `space.soft` | `R` plus the larger of 5 % of `T` and 2 GiB, no more than `R + 20 GiB`; always above `R` |
| Margin `m` | `space.margin` | the smaller of 1 % of `T` and 1 GiB |
| Hysteresis `h` | none | 1 % of `T` |

A 1 TB disk has `R` = 50 GiB and `S` = 70 GiB; a 32 GB disk has `R` = 5 GiB and
`S` = 7 GiB.

The thresholds define the state of the volume:

| State | Condition | Journal behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| normal | `F ≥ S` | previous content is kept; entries expire by their limits only |
| soft | `R ≤ F < S` | previous content is kept only when `F − extra ≥ R + m` after the write; the service releases old entries in the background until `F ≥ S + h` |
| hard | `F < R` | no previous content is kept (`no_space_for_copy`); the service releases entries at once until `F ≥ R + m`, large entries in part, largest files first |
| emergency | `F < R / 2` | as hard, with release on every processor core; commands do not wait for the service |

Before a change the journal keeps previous content of a target only when the
volume is eligible, the space service is running, the operation fits
`journal.max_op_size` and `journal.max_size`, and `F − extra ≥ R + m` and
`bytes_held + extra ≤ journal.max_size` both hold after the write, where
`extra` is the space the journal additionally occupies. Otherwise expired
entries and then old entries are released within `space.sync_budget_ms`
(1500 ms); when that is not enough, the target is changed without preservation
and the result marks it irreversible. Entries released for space are chosen by
bytes released per second of removal; pinned entries are released for space
like any other entry.

Guarantees:

- The journal never causes a user operation to fail for lack of space.
- While the space service is not running, the journal keeps no new data.
- The journal itself never lowers free space below the reserve; other
  programs can.
- A write that needs no more than `F` at its start, while `F ≥ R`, succeeds;
  in particular every write of at most `R` bytes.

Not guaranteed:

- A write that needs more than `F` but no more than `F` plus the reclaimable
  bytes succeeds only when the service releases entries before the write runs
  out of space; installers that check free space in advance see `F` only.
- After a write lowers `F` below `R`, free space returns above `R` after the
  release completes; for entries with millions of files this takes minutes.
- An external write that is larger than `F` and faster than release can run
  out of space; the reserve protects writes up to `R`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `volume` | `path` | none | Only the volume that contains this path. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `volume` |

Sizes are logical: data shared with names outside the journal through hard
links counts as zero, and on file systems that release blocks lazily `free`
grows up to a few seconds after the release.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `journal` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Report free space and the journal share of every journal volume:

```nurt example
journal.space
```

Report the volume of the home directory:

```nurt example
journal.space volume: "/home/user"
```

Report the volume that contains a project directory; the path selects its
volume and need not be the mount point:

```nurt example
journal.space volume: "/home/user/projects/app"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | no volume contains the path | give an existing path or omit `volume` |
| `E_SERVICE_NOT_RUNNING` | the space service is not running, so no volume can be measured | start the space service, then repeat the command |
| `E_IO` | free space or the journal index cannot be read | check the volume and repeat the command |

## Related

`journal.status` reports entries, limits and their sources; `journal.purge`
releases entries at once; `journal.limits` changes the step, age and size
limits.

title: journal.status
text:
# journal.status

## Synopsis

```text
journal.status [name: value]...
```

## Description

`journal.status` reports the retention state of the journal: one
`journal_state` record per volume, or for the volume that contains `volume`.
It is the only command that reports retention state; the results of other
commands state whether an operation can be undone, never for how long.

The effective limits are resolved from seven configuration levels, in
increasing precedence: built-in defaults, the system file, the user file, the
project file `.nurt.toml` (only for a trusted project), the file named by
`NURT_CONFIG`, the `NURT_JOURNAL_*` environment variables and run-time
settings of `journal.limits`. Every limit is reported with the level that set
it. A protection floor (`journal.floor.max_ops`, `journal.floor.max_age`)
raises lower values from any level; a raised limit has the source `floor`.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `active` | the journal keeps data on the volume |
| `entries` | entries that can be undone, partial entries included |
| `bytes` | logical bytes held by the journal |
| `limits` | the limits `steps`, `age` and `size`, each with `name`, `value`, `source`, `scope` and `floor` |
| `volume` | mount point of the volume |
| `oldest` | commit time of the oldest entry that can be undone |
| `oldest_id` | number of that entry |
| `reason` | why the journal is off on the volume, for example `service_down` or `network_volume`; absent when it is on |

`source` names the level that set the value: `default`, `system`, `user`,
`project`, `config_file`, `environment`, `session` (set by `journal.limits`
for the session, then `scope` is `session`) or `floor`. `floor` gives the
protection floor of `steps` and `age`; it is absent when only the project
minimum applies. `unlimited` is the value of a limit that is off.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `volume` | `path` | none | Only the journal of the volume that contains this path. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `journal_state` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `journal` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Report the journal of every volume:

```nurt example
journal.status
```

Report the journal of the volume that holds a project:

```nurt example
journal.status volume: "/home/user/project"
```

List the volumes where the journal is off:

```nurt example
journal.status |> filter active == false
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | no journal volume contains `volume` | omit `volume` or name a path on a volume with a journal |
| `E_CONFIG` | a configuration file has an invalid journal setting | correct the key named in the error |
| `E_IO` | a journal directory cannot be read | check the permissions of the journal directory |

## Related

`journal.limits`, `journal.space`, `journal.purge`, `history`.

title: last
text:
# last

## Synopsis

```text
any |> last <count>
```

## Description

`last` passes on the last `count` input records. The stage reads the whole
input and holds no more than `count` records at a time; when `count` is
larger than the record limit of the request and the input is longer than the
limit, the program stops with `E_LIMIT`.

The order, the header and the presentation hint of the stream are kept. An
input with fewer records than `count` passes on whole.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `count` | `int` | required | Number of records to keep. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `any` | `same` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `transform` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Keep the last file of a listing:

```nurt example
find "/home/user/project" |> last 1
```

Show the last two lines of a log:

```nurt example
lines "/home/user/app.log" |> last 2
```

Keep all files when there are fewer than ten:

```nurt example
find "/home/user/project" |> last 10
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | `count` is missing | write a number after `last` |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `count` is negative | use 0 or a larger number |
| `E_LIMIT` | more records must be held than the limit allows | lower `count` or narrow the input |

## Related

`first`, `skip`, `sort`.

title: lines
text:
# lines

## Synopsis

```text
lines <path> [<range>]
entry|content |> lines [<range>]
```

## Description

`lines` produces one `line` record per line of a text file. The source form
reads the given file; the encoding is detected, so UTF-16 and legacy
encodings such as Windows-1250 are decoded. The stage form reads the files of
input `entry` records and the text of input `content` records; directory
entries are passed over, and binary files are skipped and counted (notable
`binary_skipped`).

A line ends at a line feed, which may be preceded by a carriage return; a
text with carriage returns and no line feed is split at the carriage
returns. A last line without a line ending is a line, and a final line
ending does not start another line, so an empty file has no lines.

`range` selects lines by number from 1; lines past the end of the file are
not produced. Lines of a `content` record keep the numbers of the file, so
`read … lines: 10..20 |> lines` numbers them from 10.

`start` and `end` are byte offsets of the line in the file as stored,
without the line ending, also for files that are not UTF-8. They are left
out for `content` records that hold a range of lines.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | File to read in the source form. |
| `range` | `range` | `all` | Line range. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | `none` | `line` |
| `stage` | `entry`, `content` | `line` |

`line` fields: `path`, `no`, `text` (without the line ending),
`line_ending` (`lf`, `crlf`, `cr` or `none`), `etag`, `start`, `end`,
`encoding`.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Show the second and third line of a file.

```nurt example
lines "notes.txt" 2..3
```

```text expected
notes.txt:2: beta
notes.txt:3: gamma
```

Split the lines read by `read`, keeping the line numbers of the file.

```nurt example
read "notes.txt" lines: 3..4 |> lines
```

```text expected
notes.txt:3: gamma
notes.txt:4: delta
```

Show the first line of every text file found.

```nurt example
find "." glob: "*.txt" |> lines 1
```

A response that leaves lines out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | No file in the source form. | Give `path`. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | A bound of `range` is below 1. | Number lines from 1, as in `1..20`. |
| `E_TYPE` | `range` is not a range, or an input record is neither `entry` nor `content`. | Give a range such as `10..20`, or pass records of files. |
| `E_BINARY` | The file of the source form has binary content. | Use `read view: hex` for binary files. |
| `E_ENCODING` | The content is not valid in the detected encoding. | Read the file with `read encoding:` and convert it with `convert`. |
| `E_LIMIT` | The file is larger than the text limit. | Read a range of lines with `read lines:`. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | The file does not exist. | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | A relative path is given without a base directory. | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |

## Related

`read`, `search`, `replace`, `insert`.

title: list
text:
# list

## Synopsis

```text
list <path> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`list` produces one `entry` record for every entry below the directory
`path`, down to `depth` levels. The directory itself is not a record; use
`find` with `depth: 0` for a record of one path. A link to a directory is
listed as the directory it leads to.

Every record carries `depth` (1 for the direct contents) and `relative`, the
path relative to `path` with `/` separators. Names are in NFC; a stored name
that is not valid Unicode or not in NFC is kept in `raw_name`. A name that is
not valid on every supported system carries `portability` with one or more
of `windows_reserved_name`, `windows_invalid_character`,
`windows_trailing_character` and `invalid_unicode`.

A path that is not valid Unicode (on Linux, a name with the byte `0xFF`) is
written with U+FFFD in `path`, `parent` and `relative`; the record then carries
the native bytes in `raw_path`, `raw_parent` and `raw_relative`, and the target
of a link in `raw_link_target`. The next stage reads the entry from `raw_path`,
so `list ... |> remove` removes the entry that was listed.

The order depends on `view`:

| `view` | Order of the records |
|---|---|
| `flat` | by `sort` over all records; ties by path |
| `tree` | depth first, every directory before its contents; the entries of one directory by `sort` |
| `sizes` | as `tree`; every directory carries `total_size` and `file_count` |

`sort: name` compares names in NFC by code points. `sort: type` puts
directories first, then files, links and other entries. `total_size` is the
sum of the sizes of all files and links below the directory, at any depth,
and `file_count` is the number of those files; a file with several hard
links is counted once. With `view: sizes`, `sort: size` orders directories
by their totals.

On a volume that ignores letter case, `path` may differ in case from the
stored name; the listing then starts at the stored spelling, every `path`
field is in that spelling and the notable entry `case_alias` records the
given path.

An empty directory produces no records.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Directory to list. |
| `depth` | `int` | `1` | Number of directory levels to list. |
| `type` | `enum(file\|directory\|link\|any)` | `any` | Kind of entries to list. |
| `hidden` | `bool` | `true` | Include hidden entries. |
| `sort` | `enum(name\|modified\|size\|type)` | `name` | Sort key of the entries. |
| `order` | `enum(asc\|desc)` | `asc` | Sort order. |
| `view` | `enum(flat\|tree\|sizes)` | `flat` | Flat list, tree, or tree with directory size totals. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `entry`, `registry_value` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Notable entries: `permission_denied_skipped` for directories that cannot be
read, `source_unavailable` for entries that cannot be read for another
reason, `nfd_name` for names stored in another normalization form,
`portability` for names that are not portable and `case_alias` for a path
given in another letter case. Each entry gives the number of entries
concerned and a sample of up to five paths.

## Examples

List the entries of a directory, sorted by name:

```nurt example
list "/home/user/app"
```

```json fs-before
{ "format": "nurt-fs-snapshot/1", "entries": [
  { "path": "/home/user/app/README.md", "type": "file", "content_utf8": "# app\n" },
  { "path": "/home/user/app/docs/guide.md", "type": "file", "content_utf8": "guide\n" },
  { "path": "/home/user/app/src/main.go", "type": "file", "content_utf8": "package main\n" },
  { "path": "/home/user/app/src/util/util.go", "type": "file", "content_utf8": "package util\n" }
] }
```

Show two levels of the directory as a tree:

```nurt example
list "/home/user/app" depth: 2 view: tree
```

Show the directories with the total size of their contents, largest first:

```nurt example
list "/home/user/app" view: sizes sort: size order: desc
```

List the files of a directory changed most recently first:

```nurt example
list "/home/user/app/src" type: file sort: modified order: desc
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
matched 312  shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path, or list its parent directory. |
| `E_IO` | `path` is not a directory | List the parent directory, or use `find` with `depth: 0`. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | `path` cannot be read | List a directory the account may read. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `depth` is below 1 | Give a depth of 1 or more. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | a value of `type`, `sort`, `order` or `view` is unknown | Use one of the listed values. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the listing exceeds the record limit | Lower `depth`, or use `find` with `glob` or `exclude`. |

## Related

`find` selects entries by name pattern and attributes at any depth; `info`
describes one entry. `help skill: "files"` describes working with files.

title: logs
text:
# logs

## Synopsis

```text
logs [name: value]...
```

## Description

`logs` reads the log of the operating system and produces one `log_event`
record per event, newest first. It starts a pipeline. Every parameter has the
meaning of a later `filter` on the field of the same name; the stores use their
indexes to find the matching events, so a narrow query reads little of the log.

`source` and `unit` take a literal name or a glob pattern (`*`, `?`, `[...]`).
A literal name that matches no event gives an empty result with the notice
`log_unknown_name`, which lists similar names of the log. `level` is the lowest
level returned: `level: warning` returns warnings, errors and critical events.
`since` is inclusive and `until` is exclusive. `message` keeps the events whose
message matches the regular expression. `limit` bounds the number of events;
when older events remain, the execution reports the notice `log_limit_reached`
with the `cursor` of the last event, after which the older events follow.

The notice `permission_denied_skipped` is an entry of `notable` in the report.
The other notices of the command are diagnostic events of the execution whose
message starts with the code of the notice. Notices are reported when the
output ends or when the rest of the pipeline stops reading it.

### Linux

On Linux the command reads the files of the systemd journal directly, without
`journalctl` and without the systemd library. It reads the persistent journal
in `/var/log/journal/<machine-id>/` and the volatile journal in
`/run/log/journal/<machine-id>/`: active files, archived files and files
renamed after an unclean shutdown (`*.journal~`). Journals of other namespaces,
containers and remote hosts are not read. Files written with XZ, LZ4 or zstd
compression, with the keyed hash and in compact mode are supported. Entries
that journald appends while the query runs are not returned.

| Parameter | Journal fields |
|---|---|
| `source` | `SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER`, else `_COMM`, else the file name of `_EXE`, else `_TRANSPORT`; `unknown` when none is set |
| `unit` | `UNIT` for messages of the service manager, `USER_UNIT` for messages of a user manager, else `_SYSTEMD_USER_UNIT`, else `_SYSTEMD_UNIT`; a literal name without a unit suffix gets `.service`, as in `journalctl -u` |
| `level` | `PRIORITY` 0-2 is `critical`, 3 `error`, 4 `warning`, 5-6 `info`, 7 `debug`; a missing priority is 6 |

A file that is damaged, truncated or written with an unknown incompatible
feature is skipped with the notice `log_file_skipped`; the events read from it
before the defect are kept. Files that the account may not read are skipped
with the notice `permission_denied_skipped`.

### Windows

On Windows the command reads the Event Log. `unit` names an event log channel,
such as `System`, `Application`, `Security` or
`Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational`; channel names are compared
without regard to case. Without `unit`, the channels `System` and
`Application` are read. `source` names the event provider (`Provider/@Name`).
Event levels map as follows: 1 is `critical`, 2 `error`, 3 `warning`, 5
`debug`; 0, 4 and provider levels from 16 are `info`. The message is formatted
from the metadata of the provider; without metadata it holds the payload as
`name=value` pairs and the notice `log_unformatted` gives the number of such
events.

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| unknown channel | `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE`, `expected` lists the nearest channel names |
| named channel denied, such as `Security` | `E_PRIVILEGE`, `required: administrator` |
| default channel denied | notice `permission_denied_skipped` |
| event log service stopped | `E_NOT_FOUND` |

### macOS

On macOS the command reads the unified log. `unit` names a subsystem, such as
`com.example.agent`, and `source` names a process. Faults are `critical`,
errors `error`, messages of type `default` and `info` are `info`, and `debug`
messages are `debug`. The system keeps debug and info messages only for a
short time. Reading the log store of the running system requires root; a
process that runs as root and is refused needs Full Disk Access for the
terminal application.

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| not root | `E_PRIVILEGE`, `required: root` |
| root without Full Disk Access | `E_PRIVILEGE`, `required: full_disk_access` |
| messages lost by the system | notice `log_events_lost` with the count |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `source` | `text` | none | Event source: identifier, provider or subsystem. |
| `unit` | `text` | none | Service unit, event channel or category. |
| `level` | `enum(critical\|error\|warning\|info\|debug)` | `info` | Lowest level of events to return. |
| `since` | `instant` | none | Only events at or after this time. |
| `until` | `instant` | none | Only events before this time. |
| `message` | `regex` | none | Only events whose message matches this pattern. |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` | Maximum number of events, newest first. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `log_event` |

The `log_event` record holds `time`, `source`, `level` and `message`, and where
the log provides them `id`, `host`, `unit`, `pid`, `boot_id`, `cursor` and
`fields`. On Linux `id` is `MESSAGE_ID` and `fields` holds the other fields of
the entry except `MESSAGE`, `MESSAGE_ID`, `_HOSTNAME`, `_PID` and `_BOOT_ID`.

A message longer than 65536 bytes and a value of another field longer than
16384 bytes are cut at a character boundary, and fields beyond the first 128
are dropped; the event is then marked as truncated. A message that is not
valid UTF-8 is decoded with replacement characters.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Show the errors of one service:

```nurt example
logs unit: "ssh" level: error
```

Find failed logins in the messages of `sshd`:

```nurt example
logs source: "sshd" message: /Failed password/ limit: 20
```

Show the five newest warnings and errors of the system:

```nurt example
logs level: warning |> first 5
```

Read the events of all timer units:

```nurt example
logs unit: "*.timer" level: debug
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the kept events first and then
continues the query from the cursor of the last event, so that parts neither
overlap nor skip events that arrive later.

```text
shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | The system has no log that `logs` reads, such as a Linux system without a systemd journal. | Read text log files such as `/var/log/syslog` with `read`. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | No log file is readable by the account. | On Linux add the account to the group `systemd-journal` or `adm`, or run as root. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The log needs a privilege the process does not have: a named Windows channel such as `Security`, or the macOS log store. | Run with administrator rights on Windows; run as root, and grant Full Disk Access if needed, on macOS. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | `unit` names a Windows channel that does not exist; `expected` lists the nearest names. | Use one of the listed channels. |
| `E_OS_ONLY` | The operating system is not Linux, Windows or macOS. | Read text log files with `read`. |
| `E_FORMAT` | No log file has a readable format; `files` lists the files with the class of their defect. | Check the files; files written by a newer systemd need a newer release of Danaco Nurt. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | A parameter has a value of the wrong form, such as a cursor of another system. | Use a cursor returned by `logs` on the same system. |
| `E_REGEX` | The pattern of `message` is not a valid regular expression. | Correct the pattern. |
| `E_PATTERN_SYNTAX` | The glob pattern of `source` or `unit` is malformed. | Close the bracket or escape the special character. |
| `E_LIMIT` | `limit` is below 1 or above 100000. | Give a `limit` within the range, or narrow the query with `since` and `until`. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | The execution was cancelled between two events. | Run the program again. |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | The time limit of the program elapsed while the log was read. | Narrow the query with `since`, `unit` or `source`. |

## Related

`services` lists the services whose `unit` names `logs` accepts. `filter`,
`group` and `sort` process the `log_event` records further. The `system` group
page lists the other commands of the group.

title: modules.load
text:
# modules.load

## Synopsis

```text
modules.load <name> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`modules.load` loads a kernel module with `modprobe` on Linux; `params` are passed as `name=value`. A module that is already loaded is `unchanged`. `lsmod` decides; `-` and `_` are the same character in the name of a module.

Rights: the command accepts `privilege`; write `privilege: elevated` when the account that runs Nurt is not the administrator. A program that fails for lack of rights ends the command with `E_PERMISSION`, and `privilege: auto` repeats it once elevated. An elevated entry is undone by the same elevated process.

`undo` runs `modules.unload`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text` | required | Module name. |
| `params` | `list<text>` | none | Module parameters as name=value. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible_if_preserved` |
| Implementation | `system_program` |
| Reversibility conditions | Undo unloads the module. |
| Operating systems | `linux` |
| External use | `system_program`: `modprobe`, `lsmod`; Modules are listed with lsmod and loaded with modprobe. |

## Examples

Load a module.

```nurt example
modules.load "br_netfilter" privilege: elevated
```

Load a module with a parameter.

```nurt example
modules.load "nf_conntrack" params: ["hashsize=65536"] privilege: elevated
```

Run the load with elevated rights; adding the call parameter `preview: true` shows the effect first.

```nurt example
modules.load "overlay" privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_OS_ONLY` | The system is not Linux. | Use the tools of the system. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The module does not exist. | Check the name. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The account lacks the rights of the administrator. | Add `privilege: elevated`. |
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The system program of the command is not installed. | Install the program named in the message. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The system program ended with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`modules.unload`, `sysctl.set`.

title: modules.unload
text:
# modules.unload

## Synopsis

```text
modules.unload <name>
```

## Description

`modules.unload` unloads a kernel module with `modprobe -r` on Linux. A module that is not loaded is `unchanged`.

Rights: the command accepts `privilege`; write `privilege: elevated` when the account that runs Nurt is not the administrator. A program that fails for lack of rights ends the command with `E_PERMISSION`, and `privilege: auto` repeats it once elevated. An elevated entry is undone by the same elevated process.

`undo` runs `modules.load`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text` | required | Module name. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible_if_preserved` |
| Implementation | `system_program` |
| Reversibility conditions | Undo loads the module. |
| Operating systems | `linux` |
| External use | `system_program`: `modprobe`, `lsmod`; Modules are listed with lsmod and unloaded with modprobe -r. |

## Examples

Unload a module.

```nurt example
modules.unload "dummy" privilege: elevated
```

Unload and show the effect.

```nurt example
modules.unload "dummy" privilege: elevated |> select target
```

Run the unload with elevated rights; adding the call parameter `preview: true` shows the effect first.

```nurt example
modules.unload "dummy" privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_OS_ONLY` | The system is not Linux. | Use the tools of the system. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The module is in use. | Stop its users first. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The account lacks the rights of the administrator. | Add `privilege: elevated`. |
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The system program of the command is not installed. | Install the program named in the message. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The system program ended with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`modules.load`.

title: mount
text:
# mount

## Synopsis

```text
mount <device> <target> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`mount` mounts a device or volume with `mount` on Linux and macOS and `mountvol` on Windows (drive letters and folder mounts). The mount point is read first: the same device already mounted there is `unchanged`, another device is `E_IN_USE`. With `persistent: true` on Linux the line of `/etc/fstab` for the mount point is written or replaced; the edit is a file change of the journal. macOS does not support `persistent`.

Rights: the command accepts `privilege`; write `privilege: elevated` when the account that runs Nurt is not the administrator. A program that fails for lack of rights ends the command with `E_PERMISSION`, and `privilege: auto` repeats it once elevated. An elevated entry is undone by the same elevated process.

`undo` runs `unmount`; the journal restores `/etc/fstab`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `device` | `text` | required | Device, volume or source of the mount. |
| `target` | `text` | required | Mount point: a directory, or a drive letter or folder on Windows. |
| `type` | `text` | none | File system type; detected by the system when omitted. |
| `options` | `list<text>` | none | Mount options. |
| `persistent` | `bool` | `false` | Also write the mount to /etc/fstab (Linux); the file is journaled. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible_if_preserved` |
| Implementation | `system_program` |
| Reversibility conditions | Undo unmounts the target; the edit of /etc/fstab is restored by the journal. |
| External use | `system_program`: `mount`, `mountvol`; Mounts use mount on Linux and macOS and mountvol on Windows. |

## Examples

Mount a device.

```nurt example
mount "/dev/sdb1" "/srv/data" type: "ext4" privilege: elevated
```

Mount read-only and keep the mount after a restart.

```nurt example
mount "/dev/sdb1" "/srv/data" type: "ext4" options: ["ro", "noatime"] persistent: true privilege: elevated
```

Mount a USB stick for one account.

```nurt example
mount "/dev/sdc1" "/mnt/usb" type: "vfat" options: ["uid=1000"] privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_IN_USE` | Another device is mounted at the mount point. | Unmount it first. |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | `persistent` on macOS. | Omit `persistent`. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The account lacks the rights of the administrator. | Add `privilege: elevated`. |
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The system program of the command is not installed. | Install the program named in the message. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The system program ended with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`unmount`, `disks`, `disks.format`.

title: move
text:
# move

## Synopsis

```text
move <from>... [<to>] (to: <path> | into: <path>) [name: value]...
entry |> move [<to>] (to: <path> | into: <path>) [name: value]...
```

## Description

`move` moves files, symbolic links, junctions and directory trees to another
path. The source form takes the paths of `from`; the stage form takes
`entry` records. `to` and `into` exclude each other, and one of them is
required.

`to` is the new path of the entry. When `to` names an existing directory,
the entry is moved inside it under its own name and the result reports
`to_is_dir`. `into` always names a directory that receives the entries; it
is created with its missing parents. Several sources need a directory:
`into`, or `to` naming an existing directory. `to` is evaluated per input
record in the stage form.

Every entry is moved as a whole: a directory with its content, a link as a
link. Within one volume the entry is renamed. Between volumes the journal
copies the entry and removes the source after the copy is complete; the
result reports `cross_device`. A move that changes only the letter case of
the name on a volume that does not distinguish case renames the entry
itself.

`on_conflict` decides what happens to an existing file or link at the
destination: `overwrite` replaces it, `skip` keeps it and leaves the source
in place, `error` fails before anything changes. An existing directory is
never replaced. A directory cannot move into itself, and a source inside
another source of the same call is rejected.

An entry record with `etag` must still have that entity tag; a changed entry
fails with `E_STALE` before anything changes. Empty input moves nothing and
reports `nothing_matched`.

| Notable code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `to_is_dir` | `to` named an existing directory, which received the entry |
| `cross_device` | the entry moved to another volume as a copy and a removal |
| `case_collision` | the destination differs from an existing name only in letter case on a volume that does not distinguish case |
| `nothing_matched` | the input had no entries |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | `list<path>` | required | Files and directories to move in the source form. |
| `to` | `path` | one of `destination` | Target path; an existing directory receives the entry. |
| `into` | `path` | one of `destination` | Target directory, created when missing. |
| `on_conflict` | `enum(overwrite\|skip\|error)` | `overwrite` | Behaviour when the target file exists. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | `none` | `effect` |
| `stage` | `entry` | `effect` |

The `effect` record has one `change` with action `rename` per moved entry,
with `path` set to the source and `to` to the destination, and one `change`
per directory created for `into`. Its `summary` counts `moved`,
`overwritten`, `skipped` and `cross_device`.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Move a file into an existing directory:

```nurt example
move "/home/user/report.txt" "/home/user/done"
```

```text expected
move: 1 target, moved 1, notable: to_is_dir
```

Move two files into a directory that does not exist yet:

```nurt example
move "/srv/a.log" into: "/srv/old"
```

Move a file to another volume:

```nurt example
move "/data/export.csv" "/mnt/usb/export.csv"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | no source, or neither `to` nor `into` | give `from` and a destination |
| `E_PARAM_CONFLICT` | both `to` and `into`, or several sources and `to` is not an existing directory | give one destination; use `into` for several sources |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | a source or the directory of `to` does not exist | check the path or use `into` |
| `E_EXISTS` | the target exists with `on_conflict: error`, is an existing directory, or two sources share one target | choose another destination or `on_conflict` value |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | a directory moved into itself, a source that is its own target, or a source inside another source | move only the enclosing directory |
| `E_STALE` | an input entry changed since it was read | read the entries again |
| `E_IN_USE` | Windows: an entry is open in another process; the error lists the processes | close the entry there |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | a relative path without a base directory | give an absolute path or set `base` |

## Related

`rename`, `copy`, `remove`, `find`, `list`.

title: network.dns_set
text:
# network.dns_set

## Synopsis

```text
network.dns_set <servers> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`network.dns_set` sets the name servers and, with `search`, the search domains of an interface. An empty list of `servers` returns the interface to automatic servers. `search` left out keeps the search domains.

| System | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Linux with systemd-resolved | `resolvectl dns`, `resolvectl domain`, `resolvectl revert`; `interface` defaults to the interface of the default route |
| Linux otherwise | the file `/etc/resolv.conf`, rewritten through the journal so that `undo` restores the file; the other lines of the file are kept; a link is refused with `E_UNSUPPORTED` |
| macOS | `networksetup -setdnsservers` and `-setsearchdomains`; `interface` is the name of the network service |
| Windows | `Set-DnsClientServerAddress` for the interface alias, `Set-DnsClientGlobalSetting` for the search domains |

When the servers and domains already hold, nothing is changed. `undo` sets the previous servers and domains with `network.dns_set`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `servers` | `list<text>` | required | IP addresses of the name servers, in order; an empty list means automatic. |
| `search` | `list<text>` | none | Search domains; unchanged when omitted. |
| `interface` | `text` | none | Interface or network service; the interface of the default route when omitted on Linux. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| Reversibility conditions | `undo` sets the previous servers and domains; changes of /etc/resolv.conf are restored by the journal. |
| External use | `system_program`: `ip`, `route`, `netstat`, `resolvectl`, `networksetup`, `powershell`; Routes and DNS are read and changed through ip, route, netstat, resolvectl and networksetup, and through the NetTCPIP and DnsClient cmdlets of PowerShell on Windows. |

## Examples

Use two public name servers on an interface.

```nurt example
network.dns_set ["1.1.1.1", "8.8.8.8"] interface: "eth0" privilege: elevated
```

Set servers and search domains.

```nurt example
network.dns_set ["198.51.100.2"] search: ["corp.example.com"] interface: "eth0" privilege: elevated
```

Return an interface to automatic servers.

```nurt example
network.dns_set [] interface: "eth0" privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | A server is not an IP address or a domain is not a domain name. | Correct the value. |
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | `interface` is needed and not given. | Name the interface. |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | `/etc/resolv.conf` is a link that another service manages. | Set the DNS in that service or enable systemd-resolved. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The program of the system refused the change for want of rights. | Repeat the call with `privilege: elevated`. |

## Related

`network.route_add`, `network.route_remove`.

title: network.interfaces
text:
# network.interfaces

## Synopsis

```text
network.interfaces
```

## Description

`network.interfaces` returns one `network_interface` record per network
interface of the host, ordered by name. Addresses of an alias such as
`eth0:1` belong to the interface `eth0`. The default gateway of an interface
is taken from the IPv4 routing table, otherwise from the IPv6 routing table.

The fields are read from the following interfaces of the operating system.

| System | Addresses | State, MAC, MTU, kind | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux | `getifaddrs` | `/sys/class/net/<name>/{operstate,flags,address,mtu,type}`; `wireless` or `phy80211` gives `wireless`, a missing `device` gives `virtual` | `/proc/net/route`, `/proc/net/ipv6_route` |
| macOS | `getifaddrs` | link-layer entries of `getifaddrs` and their interface data; the link type and the name prefix give the kind | routing table read through `sysctl` (`NET_RT_FLAGS`) |
| Windows | `GetAdaptersAddresses` | the adapter entry; the interface type gives the kind | gateways of the adapter, IPv4 first |

On Linux, an `operstate` of `unknown`, as reported by the loopback interface
and some virtual interfaces, is resolved by the `IFF_UP` flag.

## Parameters

The command has no parameters.

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `network_interface` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

List all interfaces:

```nurt example
network.interfaces
```

```text
network_interface  lo    127.0.0.1/8, ::1/128         up  loopback
network_interface  eth0  192.0.2.10/24, 2001:db8::10/64  up  ethernet  gateway 192.0.2.1
```

List the interfaces that are up and have a default gateway:

```nurt example
network.interfaces |> filter up and gateway != null
```

Show the hardware addresses of the wireless interfaces:

```nurt example
network.interfaces |> filter kind == "wireless" |> select name mac
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_IO` | The system refuses the list of interfaces, or `/sys/class/net` cannot be read on Linux. | Check the state of the system and run the program again. |
| `E_OS_ONLY` | The system is not Linux, macOS or Windows. | Run the program on a supported system. |

## Related

`network.ping`, `network.resolve`, `ports`.

title: network.ping
text:
# network.ping

## Synopsis

```text
network.ping <host> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`network.ping` sends `count` ICMP echo requests to `host`, one second apart,
and returns one `ping_result` record with the number of replies and the
round-trip times. A host name is resolved by the resolver of the operating
system, which also reads the hosts file; the first address is used. An
address is used as given, IPv4 or IPv6.

A request without a reply within `timeout` counts as lost. Replies are
matched to their requests by sequence number and by a random token in the
payload, so replies to other programs are ignored.

| System | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Linux | ICMP datagram socket (`SOCK_DGRAM` with `IPPROTO_ICMP` or `IPPROTO_ICMPV6`) |
| macOS | ICMP datagram socket |
| Windows | `IcmpSendEcho` for IPv4, `Icmp6SendEcho2` for IPv6 |

Raw sockets are not used.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `host` | `text` | required | Host name or address. |
| `count` | `int` | `4` | Number of requests. |
| `timeout` | `duration` | `2s` | Time to wait for each reply. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `ping_result` |

Progress events of phase `echo` report the requests sent.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

On Linux a group of the account must be in `net.ipv4.ping_group_range`; on
macOS and Windows no privilege is required. When Linux refuses the socket,
the error names the current value of `net.ipv4.ping_group_range` and offers
a fix that allows every group.

## Examples

Send four requests to a host:

```nurt example
network.ping "example.org"
```

```text
ping_result  example.org  93.184.215.14  sent 4  received 4  loss 0
```

Send ten requests to an IPv6 address and wait up to one second for each:

```nurt example
network.ping "2001:db8::1" count: 10 timeout: 1s
```

Report only the loss and the average round trip of a gateway:

```nurt example
network.ping "192.168.1.1" count: 20 |> select loss rtt_avg
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `count` is below 1, `timeout` is zero, or `host` is empty. | Give a positive count and time limit and a host. |
| `E_NETWORK` | The host name cannot be resolved (`problem` `dns`) or a request cannot be sent (`problem` `icmp`). | Check the name and the network. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The system refuses an ICMP socket to the account. | Run the program in `fix`, which widens `net.ipv4.ping_group_range`. |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | The program reached its time limit. | Lower `count` or raise the limit of the program. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | The execution was cancelled. | Run the command again. |

## Related

`network.resolve`, `network.interfaces`, `http.request`.

title: network.resolve
text:
# network.resolve

## Synopsis

```text
network.resolve <name> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`network.resolve` sends a DNS query for `name` and returns the records of
the answer as `dns_record` records, one per record. The name is queried as
given, without search domains. An answer without records of the type gives
no records; a name that does not exist fails with `E_NOT_FOUND`.

Without `server`, the servers of the system configuration are asked in turn
until one answers: the `nameserver` lines of `/etc/resolv.conf` on Linux and
macOS (at most three, with `options timeout:` and `attempts`), and the DNS
servers of the network adapters on Windows. With `server`, only that server
is asked.

Each query is one UDP datagram. A truncated answer is repeated over TCP.
`type: any` sends one query per type, in the order A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS,
CNAME, and merges the records without duplicates; it does not send a query
of type `ANY`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text` | required | Domain name. |
| `type` | `enum(a\|aaaa\|mx\|txt\|ns\|cname\|any)` | `a` | Record type. |
| `server` | `text` | none | DNS server to ask instead of the system resolver. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `dns_record` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Resolve the IPv4 addresses of a name:

```nurt example
network.resolve "example.org"
```

```text
dns_record  example.org  A  93.184.215.14  ttl 3600s
```

Ask a given server for the mail exchangers of a domain:

```nurt example
network.resolve "example.org" type: mx server: "192.0.2.53"
```

List the records of every supported type, ordered by type:

```nurt example
network.resolve "example.org" type: any |> sort by: type
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `type` is not one of the listed values, `name` is not a valid domain name, or `server` is not an address and cannot be resolved. | Correct the value as described in the message. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | The server answers that the name does not exist. | Check the spelling of the name. |
| `E_NETWORK` | No server answers, or every server reports a failure (`problem` `dns`, the server in `server`). | Check the network or give another server with `server`. |
| `E_IO` | The system configuration exists but cannot be read. | Check the permissions of `/etc/resolv.conf`. |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | The program reached its time limit. | Raise the limit of the program. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | The execution was cancelled. | Run the command again. |

## Related

`network.ping`, `network.interfaces`, `http.request`.

title: network.route_add
text:
# network.route_add

## Synopsis

```text
network.route_add <destination> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`network.route_add` adds a route to the routing table: `ip route add` on Linux, `route add` on macOS and `New-NetRoute` on Windows. `destination` is a network in CIDR form, a host address or `default`. A route needs a `gateway` or an `interface`. When the table already holds a route with the same destination, next hop, interface and metric, nothing is changed and the report states `unchanged`. `undo` removes the route with `network.route_remove`.

Routes and DNS are read before the change. The report holds the state before and after (`via=<gateway> dev=<interface> metric=<n>` for a route, `servers=<list>;search=<list>` for DNS), and `undo` restores it.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `destination` | `text` | required | Network in CIDR form, a host address or default. |
| `gateway` | `text` | none | Next hop. Required unless interface is given. |
| `interface` | `text` | none | Interface of the route. |
| `metric` | `int` | none | Metric of the route. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| Reversibility conditions | `undo` removes the route; a route that already exists is left alone. |
| External use | `system_program`: `ip`, `route`, `netstat`, `resolvectl`, `networksetup`, `powershell`; Routes and DNS are read and changed through ip, route, netstat, resolvectl and networksetup, and through the NetTCPIP and DnsClient cmdlets of PowerShell on Windows. |

## Examples

Route a network through a gateway.

```nurt example
network.route_add "10.9.0.0/16" gateway: "203.0.113.5" privilege: elevated
```

Route a network over an interface with a metric.

```nurt example
network.route_add "10.20.0.0/16" interface: "eth0" metric: 200 privilege: elevated
```

Set the default route.

```nurt example
network.route_add "default" gateway: "203.0.113.1" privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | A value is not an address, a network or an interface name. | Correct the value. |
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | Neither `gateway` nor `interface` is given. | Name the next hop or the interface. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The program of the system refused the change for want of rights. | Repeat the call with `privilege: elevated`. |

## Related

`network.route_remove` removes routes and `network.dns_set` sets name servers.

title: network.route_remove
text:
# network.route_remove

## Synopsis

```text
network.route_remove <destination> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`network.route_remove` removes the routes that match `destination` and, when given, `gateway`, `interface` and `metric`: `ip route del` on Linux, `route delete` on macOS and `Remove-NetRoute` on Windows. A call that matches no route fails with `E_NOT_FOUND`. Every removed route is recorded with its next hop, interface and metric, and `undo` adds it again with `network.route_add`.

Routes and DNS are read before the change. The report holds the state before and after (`via=<gateway> dev=<interface> metric=<n>` for a route, `servers=<list>;search=<list>` for DNS), and `undo` restores it.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `destination` | `text` | required | Network in CIDR form, a host address or default. |
| `gateway` | `text` | none | Next hop. Only routes through this next hop. |
| `interface` | `text` | none | Interface of the route. |
| `metric` | `int` | none | Metric of the route. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| Reversibility conditions | `undo` adds the routes that were removed. |
| External use | `system_program`: `ip`, `route`, `netstat`, `resolvectl`, `networksetup`, `powershell`; Routes and DNS are read and changed through ip, route, netstat, resolvectl and networksetup, and through the NetTCPIP and DnsClient cmdlets of PowerShell on Windows. |

## Examples

Remove a route to a network.

```nurt example
network.route_remove "10.9.0.0/16" privilege: elevated
```

Remove the route that uses one next hop.

```nurt example
network.route_remove "10.9.0.0/16" gateway: "203.0.113.5" privilege: elevated
```

Remove the route of one interface.

```nurt example
network.route_remove "10.20.0.0/16" interface: "eth0" privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | No route matches. | Read the routes of the system. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | A value is not an address, a network or an interface name. | Correct the value. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The program of the system refused the change for want of rights. | Repeat the call with `privilege: elevated`. |

## Related

`network.route_add`, `network.dns_set`.

title: next
text:
# next

## Synopsis

```text
next [<id>] [<count>] [name: value]...
```

## Description

`next` returns the next part of a result that an earlier response shortened.
The first response of a command stays short; one more call returns the next
part, then the next, until the end. A response that leaves lines, records,
bytes or the end of long lines out carries the field `continuation` and its
text ends with the hint "more: next".

| Field of `continuation` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | short identifier, `c1`, `c2`, … within the session of the console |
| `unit` | `lines`, `records` or `bytes` |
| `shown` | units in the responses given so far |
| `remaining` | units not yet given; `-1` when not known in advance |
| `cut_lines` | lines of the shown part that were shortened |

The hint is "more: next" when the continuation is the latest one and
"more: next c3" otherwise. The call forms are:

| Call | Short form | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `next` | `next` | next part of the latest continuation |
| `next id: c3` | `next c3` | next part of the continuation `c3` |
| `next count: 200` | `next 200` | a part of 200 units; the default is the size of the first response |
| `next c3 count: 200` | `next c3 200` | both |
| `next id: c3 all: true` | `next c3 all` | everything that is left of `c3` |
| `next id: c3 full_lines: true` | `next c3 full` | the cut lines of `c3`, whole |
| `next all: true` | `next all` | everything that is left |
| `next full_lines: true` | `next full` | the lines of the last shown part that were cut, whole |

The identifier, the count and the words `all` and `full` are positional; a
bare word `all` or `full` stands for the parameter of the same meaning. The
long forms stay valid and give the same result.

The part has the same record type as the first response of a reading command
and the record type `line` for the output of `run`, so a pipeline continues it:
`next |> filter severity == "error"`. `next` never computes the result again.
It reads the rest from the source that the first response kept:

| Command | Source of the continuation |
|---|---|
| `run` | the output file of the run (lines): the lines between the head and the tail of the response; a selection of lines is continued from the first line of the file |
| `search`, `find`, `list`, `read`, `lines`, `diff`, `git.log`, `git.diff`, `git.blame`, `history`, `processes`, `ports`, `services`, `package.list`, `package.search`, `query`, `sql` and other reading commands | the computed result kept in the state directory, in the order of the response |
| `logs` | the cursor of the query at the time of the first response, so that the parts neither overlap nor skip events that arrive later |
| a pipeline | the result of its last stage |

Details of the parts. `next` after the last lines of a result that cut lines
reads the cut lines whole, as `next full` does; `next full` on a result
without cut lines gives an empty part, and on the continuation of a query with
a cursor (`logs`) it fails with `E_INVALID_VALUE`. A result that shows a
selection of lines (`show: errors`) is continued from the first line of the
file, so its parts repeat the lines already shown. A `run` whose `stdout` and
`stderr` are both shortened continues one stream after the other. When
one program has several stages that cut their output (for example two `run`),
the first of them in program order is continued; the others are reachable
through their own output files. `next` runs a query with a cursor (`logs`)
again under the options of the first call (`session`, `base`, `timeout`). A
continuation belongs to the session that made it: another session gets
`E_CONTINUATION_EXPIRED`. A result larger than `continuation.max_size` is not
kept; the response has no `continuation`, and a notice explains why.

`next` is a reading command: it changes nothing, writes no journal entry and
costs no effect in `E_ONE_EFFECT`. The answer carries its own `continuation`
with the same `id` while something remains; the last part has `remaining: 0`
and no hint. The lifetime and the space of the kept results are set by
`continuation.max_age` (1 hour), `continuation.max_count` (50) and
`continuation.max_size` (256 MiB); the oldest continuation is removed first,
and the results are removed at the end of the session of the console.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `int \| field \| text` | the latest continuation | Continuation to read, `c3`; also a count (`next 200`) or the words `all` and `full`. |
| `count` | `int \| field \| text` | the size of the first response | Units in the part. |
| `all` | `bool` | `false` | Read everything that is left. |
| `full_lines` | `bool` | `false` | Read the lines of the last shown part that were cut, whole. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `any` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Read the next part of the latest shortened result; without a kept result the
call fails with `E_CONTINUATION_EXPIRED`:

```nurt example
next
```

```text expected
E_CONTINUATION_EXPIRED
```

Read 200 units of the continuation `c3`:

```nurt example
next c3 200
```

Read everything that is left of the latest continuation and count it:

```nurt example
next all |> count
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_CONTINUATION_EXPIRED` | the continuation is older than `continuation.max_age`, was removed by `continuation.max_count` or `continuation.max_size`, or none is kept; `next_steps` holds the call that produced it | run the call from `next_steps` again |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `count` is below 1, or the identifier is not of the form `cN` | give a count of at least 1 and an identifier such as `c3` |

## Related

`run`, `search`, `find`, `list`, `logs`, `help skill: "large-results"`.

title: notebook.cells
text:
# notebook.cells

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.cells <path> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`notebook.cells` produces one `cell` record for each selected cell of the
notebook `path`, in the order of the cells. Every record carries `index`
(from 0), `id` (nbformat 4.5 and later), `cell_type`, `source`,
`execution_count` of code cells and `etag`, the entity tag of the file.

Without `index`, `id` and `find`, every cell is listed as an outline: `source`
is the first non-blank line and `metadata` is left out. With any of them,
the selected cells are listed in full, with the whole source and the
metadata. A `view` given explicitly overrides that choice.

`index` and `id` select cells together: a cell is listed when its index lies
in the range or its identifier is listed. The start of `index` must name an
existing cell; the end may lie past the last cell. `cell_type` keeps only
cells of that type. `find` keeps only cells in which the text or regular
expression occurs, in the source or, with `scope: outputs`, in the text of
the outputs. Regular expressions use the dialect of `search`.

`outputs` sets the detail of the outputs of code cells: `summary` adds
`outputs_summary` with the number and kinds of outputs, for example
`1 output: stream stdout`; `text` also lists each output reduced to its type,
stream name and text, without images and other binary data; `full` lists the
outputs as stored.

A notebook without cells produces no records.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `index` | `range` | none | Cells to return by index, counted from 0. |
| `id` | `list<text>` | none | Cells to return by identifier. |
| `cell_type` | `enum(code\|markdown\|raw)` | none | Only cells of this type. |
| `outputs` | `enum(none\|summary\|text\|full)` | `none` | Detail of cell outputs returned. |
| `find` | `text \| regex` | none | Only cells containing this text or pattern. |
| `scope` | `enum(source\|outputs)` | `source` | Part of the cell that find searches. |
| `view` | `enum(outline\|full)` | `outline` | Outline or full content when no cells are selected. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `cell` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

List the outline of every cell:

```nurt example
notebook.cells "/home/user/sales.ipynb"
```

```text expected
0  markdown  intro  # Sales
1  code      load   import pandas as pd
2  code      plot   df.plot(x="month", y="total")
```

Show one cell in full with the text of its outputs:

```nurt example
notebook.cells "/home/user/sales.ipynb" index: 1 outputs: text
```

List the cells whose source calls a `read_` function:

```nurt example
notebook.cells "/home/user/sales.ipynb" find: /read_\w+/
```

Summarize the outputs of the code cells:

```nurt example
notebook.cells "/home/user/sales.ipynb" cell_type: code outputs: summary
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | the start of `index` lies past the last cell | List the outline first to see the valid indexes. |
| `E_ARG` | no cell has an identifier of `id` | Use an identifier from the outline; the message names the closest ones. |
| `E_REGEX` | `find` is not a valid regular expression | Correct the pattern at the reported position. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | a value of `cell_type`, `outputs`, `scope` or `view` is unknown | Use one of the listed values. |

## Related

`read` shows a notebook as `content` with its cells; `notebook.replace`,
`notebook.insert` and `notebook.ops` change cells. `help skill: "notebooks"`
describes working with notebooks.

title: notebook.clear_outputs
text:
# notebook.clear_outputs

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.clear_outputs <path>
```

## Description

`notebook.clear_outputs` sets `outputs` to an empty list and
`execution_count` to `null` in the selected code cells: by default every
cell, otherwise the cells whose index lies in the range `index` or the cells
with the identifiers `id`. Markdown and raw cells have no outputs and are not
changed; a code cell that already has no outputs and no counter keeps its
text. A notebook without outputs is not written.

The `effect` record carries the counter `cells_cleared`, the number of cells
that changed.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `index` | `range` | `all` | Cells to clear by index, counted from 0. |
| `id` | `list<text>` | none | Cells to clear by identifier. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Clear the outputs of every cell:

```nurt example
notebook.clear_outputs "/home/user/sales.ipynb"
```

Clear the outputs of the cell at index 1:

```nurt example
notebook.clear_outputs "/home/user/sales.ipynb" index: 1
```

Clear the image output of the cell `plot`:

```nurt example
notebook.clear_outputs "/home/user/sales.ipynb" id: ["plot"]
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | a bound of `index` names no cell | Give indexes listed by `notebook.cells`. |
| `E_ARG` | no cell has an identifier of `id` | Use identifiers listed by `notebook.cells`. |
| `E_PARAM_CONFLICT` | both `index` and `id` are given | Give one of them. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells and their identifiers; `notebook.ops`
applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

title: notebook.copy
text:
# notebook.copy

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.copy <path> from: <int> to: <int>
```

## Description

`notebook.copy` inserts a copy of the cell at index `from` at index `to`,
which may be any position from 0 to the number of cells. The copy repeats the
text of the original exactly, outputs and metadata included, except for a new
identifier when the notebook uses identifiers.

The `effect` record carries the counter `cells_copied` and, in `after`, the
`index` and `id` of the copy.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `from` | `int` | required | Index of the cell to copy. |
| `to` | `int` | required | Index of the copy. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.
