## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Copy the cell `load` directly after itself:

```nurt example
notebook.copy "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 1 to: 2
```

Repeat the first cell of a notebook in nbformat 4.4, whose cells have no
identifiers:

```nurt example
notebook.copy "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 0 to: 0
```

Copying a cell that does not exist fails with `E_OUT_OF_RANGE`:

```nurt example
notebook.copy "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 9 to: 0
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | `from` names no cell, or `to` is greater than the number of cells | Give indexes listed by `notebook.cells`. |

## Related

applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

title: notebook.export
text:
# notebook.export

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.export <path> to: <path> format: <enum(script|markdown|text)>
```

## Description

`notebook.export` writes the notebook `path` to the new file `to`:

| `format` | Content |
|---|---|
| `script` | A script in the language of the kernel in the percent format: each cell starts with a `%%` marker comment; Markdown and raw cells become comments, with the marker `[markdown]` or `[raw]`. |
| `markdown` | Markdown cells as written, code cells as fenced blocks in the language of the kernel, each followed by fenced `text` blocks with the text of its outputs; raw cells as written. |
| `text` | The sources of all cells. |

Cells are separated by an empty line, and the file ends with one line break;
a notebook without cells gives an empty file. The language comes from
`metadata.language_info.name`, otherwise from `metadata.kernelspec.language`;
the comment marker of a script is `#`, `//`, `--`, `%` or `;;` by language.
Images and other binary outputs are left out. The notebook itself is not
changed.

The `effect` record carries the counters `files_created` and
`cells_exported`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `to` | `path` | required | File to create. |
| `format` | `enum(script\|markdown\|text)` | required | Format of the exported file. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Export the notebook as a Python script:

```nurt example
notebook.export "/home/user/sales.ipynb" to: "/home/user/sales.py" format: script
```

```text expected
# %% [markdown]
# # Sales
# Monthly totals.

# %%
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(len(df), "rows")

# %%
df.plot(x="month", y="total")
```

Export the notebook as Markdown with the text of the outputs:

```nurt example
notebook.export "/home/user/sales.ipynb" to: "/home/user/sales.md" format: markdown
```

Export the sources of all cells as text:

```nurt example
notebook.export "/home/user/sales.ipynb" to: "/home/user/sales.txt" format: text
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_EXISTS` | `to` already exists | Export to a new file, or remove the existing one first. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | the directory of `to` does not exist | Create the directory first. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | `format` is unknown | Use `script`, `markdown` or `text`. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells; `read` shows a notebook as `content` with
its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

title: notebook.insert
text:
# notebook.insert

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.insert <path> cell_type: <enum(code|markdown|raw)> source: <text>
```

## Description

`notebook.insert` adds one cell to the notebook `path`: at `index`, directly
after the cell with the identifier `after_id`, or after the last cell when
neither is given. The cell at `index` and the cells after it move down by
one.

The new cell has empty `metadata`; a code cell also has `execution_count:
null` and no outputs. Its `source` is stored in the form the other cells use,
a list of lines or a single string. When the notebook is in nbformat 4.5 or
later, or its cells already have identifiers, the new cell gets a new
identifier of eight hexadecimal digits that no other cell has.

The `effect` record carries the counter `cells_inserted` and, in `after`,
the `index` and `id` of the new cell.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `cell_type` | `enum(code\|markdown\|raw)` | required | Type of the new cell. |
| `source` | `text` | required | Source of the new cell. |
| `index` | `int` | the end of the notebook | Position of the new cell, counted from 0. |
| `after_id` | `text` | none | Insert after the cell with this identifier. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Append a Markdown cell:

```nurt example
notebook.insert "/home/user/sales.ipynb" cell_type: markdown source: "## Totals"
```

Insert a code cell before the cell `load`, at index 1:

```nurt example
notebook.insert "/home/user/sales.ipynb" index: 1 cell_type: code source: "import numpy as np"
```

Insert a code cell after the cell `load`:

```nurt example
notebook.insert "/home/user/sales.ipynb" after_id: "load" cell_type: code source: "df.describe()"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | `index` is negative or greater than the number of cells | Give an index from 0 to the number of cells. |
| `E_ARG` | no cell has the identifier `after_id` | Use an identifier listed by `notebook.cells`. |
| `E_PARAM_CONFLICT` | both `index` and `after_id` are given | Give one of them. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | `cell_type` is unknown | Use `code`, `markdown` or `raw`. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells and their identifiers; `notebook.ops`
applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

# notebook.move

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.move <path> from: <int> to: <int>
```

## Description

`notebook.move` moves the cell at index `from` so that it ends at index `to`;
the cells in between shift by one. Both indexes name existing cells. The
moved cell and every other cell keep their text; only the order changes.
Moving a cell to its own index changes nothing.

The `effect` record carries the counter `cells_moved`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `from` | `int` | required | Current index of the cell. |
| `to` | `int` | required | New index of the cell. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Move the last cell to the front:

```nurt example
notebook.move "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 2 to: 0
```

Swap the first two cells:

```nurt example
notebook.move "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 0 to: 1
```

Moving past the last cell fails with `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` and changes nothing:

```nurt example
notebook.move "/home/user/sales.ipynb" from: 0 to: 3
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | `from` or `to` names no cell | Give indexes listed by `notebook.cells`; `expected` shows the valid range. |

title: notebook.normalize
text:
# notebook.normalize

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.normalize <path>
```

## Description

`notebook.normalize` brings the notebook `path` to nbformat 4.5:

- `nbformat_minor` becomes 5 when it is lower, and a missing notebook
  `metadata` is added;
- every cell without a valid identifier, or with an identifier an earlier
  cell already has, gets a new identifier of eight hexadecimal digits;
- missing `metadata` and `source` are added to cells, and missing `outputs`
  and `execution_count` to code cells;
- members nbformat does not allow for the type of a cell are removed:
  `outputs` and `execution_count` of Markdown and raw cells, `attachments`
  of code cells.

Cells that need none of these changes keep their text. A second call changes
nothing and writes nothing. The other notebook commands never add
identifiers or members to cells they do not change.

The `effect` record carries the counter `cells_changed`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

Add identifiers to a notebook in nbformat 4.4, whose cells have none:

```nurt example
notebook.normalize "/home/user/sales.ipynb"
```

Give a new identifier to the second of two cells that share the identifier
`load`:

```nurt example
notebook.normalize "/home/user/sales.ipynb"
```

Add `outputs` and `execution_count` to a code cell that lacks them:

```nurt example
notebook.normalize "/home/user/sales.ipynb"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells and their identifiers; `notebook.ops`
applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

title: notebook.ops
text:
# notebook.ops

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.ops <path> changes: <list<map<any>>>
```

## Description

`notebook.ops` applies the operations of `changes` in order, each to the
result of the previous ones, and writes the notebook once. When an operation
fails, nothing is changed: the error names the operation in
`details.change`, counted from 0.

Each operation is a map with the member `action` and the parameters of the
corresponding command:

| `action` | Members | As |
|---|---|---|
| `insert` | `cell_type`, `source`, `index` or `after_id` | `notebook.insert` |
| `replace` | `index` or `id`, `source`, `cell_type`, `find`, `with`, `whole_word`, `reset_outputs` | `notebook.replace` |
| `move` | `index` or `id` of the cell, `to` | `notebook.move` |
| `copy` | `index` or `id` of the cell, `to` (directly after the original when missing) | `notebook.copy` |
| `remove` | `index` (an index or a range such as `"1..3"`) or `id` (one or a list) | `notebook.remove` |
| `clear_outputs` | `index` or `id`; every cell when both are missing | `notebook.clear_outputs` |

A member that does not apply to the action is an error. `find` may be text or
a regular expression.

The `effect` record carries the counters `operations`, `cells_inserted`,
`cells_changed`, `cells_moved`, `cells_copied`, `cells_removed`,
`cells_cleared` and `replacements`, each when it is not zero, and in `after`
a list with the `change`, `index` and `id` of every inserted or copied cell.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `changes` | `list<map<any>>` | required | Operations applied together; all succeed or none. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Insert a note after the title and remove the plot, in one write:

```nurt example
notebook.ops "/home/user/sales.ipynb" changes: [{action: "insert", after_id: "intro", cell_type: "markdown", source: "Data source: sales.csv"}, {action: "remove", id: "plot"}]
```

Rename a variable in one cell and clear every output:

```nurt example
notebook.ops "/home/user/sales.ipynb" changes: [{action: "replace", id: "load", find: "df", with: "sales", whole_word: true}, {action: "clear_outputs"}]
```

A failing operation leaves the notebook unchanged; here the second operation
names a cell that does not exist:

```nurt example
notebook.ops "/home/user/sales.ipynb" changes: [{action: "remove", index: 0}, {action: "move", index: 9, to: 0}]
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_ARG` | an operation has an unknown action, a member that does not apply, a missing or mistyped member, or names an unknown identifier; or `changes` is empty | Correct the operation named in `details.change`. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | an operation names an index outside the notebook | Correct the operation named in `details.change`; indexes refer to the result of the earlier operations. |
| `E_NO_MATCH` | the `find` of an operation occurs in no selected cell | Check the text or the cell of that operation. |
| `E_REGEX` | a regular expression or replacement template of an operation is invalid | Correct the pattern or the template. |
| `E_TYPE` | `changes` is not a list | Give a list of maps. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells and their identifiers; `notebook.ops`
applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

```text
notebook.remove <path>
```

| Reversibility | `reversible` |

preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the

```nurt example
notebook.remove "/home/user/sales.ipynb" index: 2
```

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |

| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |

title: notebook.replace
text:
# notebook.replace

## Synopsis

```text
notebook.replace <path> [name: value]...
```

## Description

The first form changes one cell, named by `index` or `id`: `source` replaces
its whole source, `cell_type` changes its type and `reset_outputs` clears its
outputs and execution counter. At least one of them is required.

The second form replaces every match of `find` with `with` within the source
of the named cell or, without `index` and `id`, within the sources of all
cells. `whole_word` matches only where the text is neither preceded nor
followed by a letter, a digit or `_`, so `df` does not match within `df2`.
With a regular expression, `with` is a template: `$1` or `${1}` inserts a
capture group by number, `$0` the whole match and `$$` a `$`. With
`reset_outputs`, the cells in which text was replaced lose their outputs. At
least one match is required.

`source` and `find` exclude each other. The source keeps the form stored in
the cell, a list of lines or a single string. A change of `cell_type` adds
`outputs` and `execution_count` when the cell becomes a code cell and removes
them, together with `attachments` of code cells, otherwise. Outputs stay
unless `reset_outputs` is set.

When both `index` and `id` are given, they must name the same cell.

The `effect` record carries the counters `cells_changed` and, with `find`,
`replacements`; the `change` record carries `replacements` too.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | Notebook file. |
| `index` | `int` | none | Cell to change by index, counted from 0. |
| `id` | `text` | none | Cell to change by identifier. |
| `source` | `text` | none | New source of the cell. |
| `cell_type` | `enum(code\|markdown\|raw)` | none | New type of the cell. |
| `find` | `text \| regex` | none | Text or pattern to replace within cell sources. |
| `with` | `text` | none | Replacement for the text matched by find. |
| `whole_word` | `bool` | `false` | Match find only as a whole word or identifier. |
| `reset_outputs` | `bool` | `false` | Clear the outputs of changed cells. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Cells and members the change does not touch keep their bytes: key order,
indentation, number notation, escapes and the layout of the file are
preserved, so a difference of the file shows only the changed cells. A call
that leaves the notebook as it was writes nothing and creates no journal
entry; its `effect` record has `targets: 0`.

## Examples

The examples use the notebook `/home/user/sales.ipynb` in nbformat 4.5 with
three cells: the Markdown cell `intro` (`# Sales`), the code cell `load`,
which reads `sales.csv` into `df` and has a stream output `12 rows`, and the
code cell `plot` with an image output.

Replace the source of the last cell:

```nurt example
notebook.replace "/home/user/sales.ipynb" index: 2 source: "df.plot(x=\"month\", y=\"total\", kind=\"bar\")"
```

Rename the variable `df` in every cell:

```nurt example
notebook.replace "/home/user/sales.ipynb" find: "df" with: "sales" whole_word: true
```

Rewrite a call with a regular expression in the cell `load`:

```nurt example
notebook.replace "/home/user/sales.ipynb" id: "load" find: /read_(\w+)/ with: "load_$1"
```

Clear the outputs of the cell `load`:

```nurt example
notebook.replace "/home/user/sales.ipynb" id: "load" reset_outputs: true
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist | Check the path. |
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative and no base directory is set | Give an absolute path or set the `base` option. |
| `E_FORMAT` | the file is not valid JSON, not UTF-8, not nbformat 4, or has repeated cell identifiers | Repair the file, convert it to nbformat 4, or run `notebook.normalize` for repeated identifiers. |
| `E_LIMIT` | the file is larger than the text limit | Raise the limit or split the notebook. |
| `E_STALE` | the notebook changed after it was read | Read the notebook again and repeat the change. |
| `E_OUT_OF_RANGE` | `index` names no cell | Give an index listed by `notebook.cells`. |
| `E_ARG` | no cell has the identifier, `index` and `id` name different cells, or the arguments are incomplete or inconsistent | Follow the message: give one cell, `source` or `find` with `with`. |
| `E_NO_MATCH` | `find` occurs in no selected cell | Check the text or the cell selection. |
| `E_REGEX` | `find` is not a valid regular expression, or `with` references a group that does not exist | Correct the pattern or the template; write `$$` for a literal `$`. |

## Related

`notebook.cells` lists the cells and their identifiers; `notebook.ops`
applies several changes in one write; `read` shows a notebook as `content`
with its cells. `help skill: "notebooks"` describes working with notebooks.

title: open_files
text:
# open_files

## Synopsis

```text
open_files <path>
```

## Description

`open_files` returns one `process` record for each process that holds
`path`, ordered by `pid`. The path must be absolute and must exist; symbolic
links in it are resolved first. A file matches the processes that use that
file. A directory matches the processes that use the directory or any path
below it.

| System | Source | `os_raw.access` |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | open descriptors, working and root directories, executable and memory maps in `/proc` | `fd`, `cwd`, `root`, `exe`, `mmap` |
| macOS | open descriptors, working and root directories, executable and mapped regions reported by the kernel | `fd`, `cwd`, `root`, `exe`, `mmap` |
| Windows | Restart Manager | not set; `os_raw.kind` is `application`, `service`, `explorer`, `console`, `critical` or `unknown` |

`os_raw.files` lists the matching paths the process uses. A file deleted while
a process keeps it open matches a directory that contained it; the record
then has `os_raw.deleted: true`. A file now at the same path is another file
and does not match.

Processes whose open files cannot be read, typically processes of other
accounts, are skipped; the report carries one `permission_denied_skipped`
note with their number. Run the console as root or as an administrator to
include them. On Windows a directory is checked through the regular files
below it, up to 10 000; beyond that the report carries a
`target_count_high` note.

The file layer uses the same search to name the holders of a file in the
`E_IN_USE` error.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `path` | required | File or directory. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `process` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Show the processes that hold a log file:

```nurt example
open_files "/var/log/app/current.log"
```

```text expected
name: app
user: app
```

Find the processes that keep a mounted volume busy:

```nurt example
open_files "/mnt/backup" |> select pid name user
```

Find the programs that lock a file on Windows:

```nurt example
open_files "C:/Users/user/Documents/report.xlsx"
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_PATH_RELATIVE` | `path` is relative. | Give an absolute path. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | `path` does not exist. | Check the path with `info`. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The process table or the Restart Manager refuses access. | Run the console as root or as an administrator. |
| `E_IO` | The process table cannot be read. | Check that `/proc` is mounted. |

## Related

`processes`, `ports`, `stop`, `accounts`.

title: package.install
text:
# package.install

## Synopsis

```text
package.install <names>... [name: value]...
```

## Description

`package.install` installs the named packages through the program of the package manager. The mark [P] in the catalog identifies this use of an external program. The program is started without a shell, with the arguments as a list, and with the variables of `run.env_defaults` followed by the variables of the manager that keep it non-interactive. No program is started during a preview.

With `version` every named package is installed in that version: `name=version` for apt and zypper, `name-version` for dnf, `name@version` for Homebrew and Scoop, and `--version` for Chocolatey and winget. pacman installs the version of the repository only and rejects `version` with `E_UNSUPPORTED`. An installed package is kept by pacman (`--needed`).

`before` comes from the package database read before the run, `after` from the database read again after it. The engine keeps the state before the change, and `undo` of the entry restores it (see Privilege).

The command needs the privilege of the manager. apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the superuser and fail with `E_PRIVILEGE` otherwise; with `privilege: elevated` the call runs through an elevation backend (`sudo`, `doas`, `run0`, or in the same process when Nurt is the administrator), and the command itself never writes `sudo`. Homebrew refuses to run as the superuser and fails with `E_PRIVILEGE` in that case. When the lock of the package database is held, the command fails with `E_IN_USE` and lists the holding processes.

A non-zero exit code of the manager ends the command with `E_STAGE_FAILED` and the end of its error output. The effect is reported as executed in that case, because the manager may have changed packages before it failed.

**Privilege.** apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the administrator. Write `privilege: elevated` on the stage to run the command through an elevation backend; without it the command fails with `E_PRIVILEGE`.

```nurt
package.install ["jq"] privilege: elevated
```

`undo` of the entry runs `package.remove` for a package that was not installed before, and installs the recorded version again for a package whose version the command changed.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `names` | `list<text>` | required | Packages to install. |
| `version` | `text` | none | Version to install. |
| `manager` | `enum(auto\|apt\|dnf\|pacman\|zypper\|brew\|winget\|choco\|scoop)` | `auto` | Package manager; auto selects the manager of the system. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

The record of each package has `target` `package:<name>`, `action`, `before` (installed version, absent when the package was not installed) and `after` (version read from the package database after the run).

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `irreversible` |
| Implementation | `package_manager` |

## Examples

Install one package.

```nurt example
package.install "ripgrep"
```

Install two packages with the apt manager.

```nurt example
package.install "curl" "jq" manager: apt
```

Install a chosen version of a package.

```nurt example
package.install "nginx" version: "1.24.0-2" manager: apt
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The program of the manager is not installed. | Install the manager or pass another `manager`. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The user lacks the privilege of the manager, or the manager refuses the superuser. | Run as root, or as a regular user for Homebrew. |
| `E_IN_USE` | The package database is locked by another process. | Wait for the listed processes to finish. |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | The manager cannot apply the request, for example a chosen version with pacman. | Omit the parameter. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The manager exited with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`package.list`, `package.search`.

title: package.list
text:
# package.list

## Synopsis

```text
package.list [name: value]...
```

## Description

`package.list` reports the installed packages of the package managers found on the system. It starts a pipeline and accepts no input. The command reads the package databases and the local repository indexes and starts no program; the mark [P] of the catalog does not apply to it.

| Manager | Database read |
|---|---|
| apt | `/var/lib/dpkg/status` and `/var/lib/dpkg/status.d/` |
| dnf, zypper | RPM database: `rpmdb.sqlite` or `Packages.db` in `/usr/lib/sysimage/rpm` or `/var/lib/rpm` |
| pacman | `local/` below `DBPath` of `/etc/pacman.conf`, by default `/var/lib/pacman` |
| brew | `Cellar` and `Caskroom` below `HOMEBREW_PREFIX`, `/opt/homebrew`, `/usr/local` or `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew` |
| winget | installation database of App Installer below `LOCALAPPDATA` and the uninstall keys of the registry |
| scoop | `apps` below `SCOOP` or `~\scoop`, and below `SCOOP_GLOBAL` |
| choco | `lib` below `ChocolateyInstall`, by default `C:\ProgramData\chocolatey` |

`name` keeps the packages whose name contains the text, without regard to case. With `outdated: true` the command reads the local repository indexes of the manager and keeps the packages for which the newest offered version of the matching architecture is greater than the installed version; `available_version` holds that version. Versions are compared by the rules of the manager: Debian policy for apt, `rpmvercmp` for dnf and zypper, `vercmp` for pacman, version with revision for Homebrew, and numeric and alphabetic segments for winget, Scoop and Chocolatey.

When several managers are found and `manager` is `auto`, each package record names its manager. Pins and priorities of apt are not evaluated. Packages of a phased update below 100 percent are not offered as newer versions. Indexes that are missing or damaged are reported as warnings and skipped; the command fails with `E_FORMAT` only when `manager` is given and every index of that manager is unreadable. Chocolatey keeps no local index, so `outdated` finds nothing for it.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text` | none | Only packages whose name contains this text. |
| `outdated` | `bool` | `false` | Only packages with a newer version available. |
| `manager` | `enum(auto\|apt\|dnf\|pacman\|zypper\|brew\|winget\|choco\|scoop)` | `auto` | Package manager; auto selects the manager of the system. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `package` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `package_manager` |

## Examples

List the installed packages whose name contains `ssl`.

```nurt example
package.list name: "ssl"
```

List the packages that have a newer version in the repositories.

```nurt example
package.list outdated: true
```

List the packages of one manager only.

```nurt example
package.list manager: pacman |> sort by: name
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
matched 1210  shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | No supported package manager was found, or the given one is not installed. | Pass `manager` of an installed manager. |
| `E_FORMAT` | Every repository index of the given manager is unreadable. | Refresh the indexes with the manager. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | The package database of the manager is missing. | Pass `manager` of an installed manager. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The package database cannot be opened by the account. | Run with an account that may read the database. |
| `E_FORMAT` | The package database is damaged. | Repair the database with the manager. |
| `E_LIMIT` | The packages exceed the record limit. | Narrow the list with `name`. |

## Related

`package.search`, `package.upgrade`.

# package.remove

## Synopsis


## Description

`package.remove` removes the named packages through the program of the package manager. The mark [P] in the catalog identifies this use of an external program. The program is started without a shell, with the arguments as a list, and with the variables of `run.env_defaults` followed by the variables of the manager that keep it non-interactive. No program is started during a preview.

Configuration files are handled by the default behaviour of the manager. Dependencies that are no longer needed stay installed.

The command needs the privilege of the manager. apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the superuser and fail with `E_PRIVILEGE` otherwise; with `privilege: elevated` the call runs through an elevation backend (`sudo`, `doas`, `run0`, or in the same process when Nurt is the administrator), and the command itself never writes `sudo`. A non-zero exit code of the manager ends the command with `E_STAGE_FAILED` and the end of its error output. The effect is reported as executed in that case, because the manager may have changed packages before it failed.

**Privilege.** apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the administrator; write `privilege: elevated` on the stage.

```nurt
package.remove ["jq"] privilege: elevated
```

`undo` of the entry installs the recorded version again, when the repository still offers it.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `names` | `list<text>` | required | Packages to remove. |
| `manager` | `enum(auto\|apt\|dnf\|pacman\|zypper\|brew\|winget\|choco\|scoop)` | `auto` | Package manager; auto selects the manager of the system. |

| Form | Input | Output |

## Effect

| Property | Value |

| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `irreversible` |
| Implementation | `package_manager` |

## Examples

Remove one package.

```nurt example
package.remove "nano"
```

```nurt example

```


| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The program of the manager is not installed. | Install the manager or pass another `manager`. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The user lacks the privilege of the manager, or the manager refuses the superuser. | Run as root, or as a regular user for Homebrew. |
| `E_IN_USE` | The package database is locked by another process. | Wait for the listed processes to finish. |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | The manager cannot apply the request, for example a chosen version with pacman. | Omit the parameter. |

title: package.search
text:
# package.search

## Synopsis

```text
package.search <query> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`package.search` finds packages in the local indexes of the repositories of the managers found on the system. It starts a pipeline and accepts no input, and it starts no program. The indexes are those the managers keep after a refresh; the command never contacts a repository.

`query` is matched against the package name and description without regard to case. A package that appears in several repositories or architectures is reported once, with the highest version. `installed` is `true` for packages that are installed; for them `version` is the installed version and `available_version` is set when the repository offers a newer one. The package whose name equals `query` comes first, the rest follow in name order.

Supported indexes: apt lists (plain, gzip, xz, bzip2, lz4 and zstd), dnf and zypper repository metadata, pacman sync databases, the Homebrew API cache, Scoop bucket manifests and the winget source index. Chocolatey keeps no local index and is reported with the warning `no_local_index`. Missing or damaged indexes are reported as warnings and skipped.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `query` | `text` | required | Search terms. |
| `manager` | `enum(auto\|apt\|dnf\|pacman\|zypper\|brew\|winget\|choco\|scoop)` | `auto` | Package manager; auto selects the manager of the system. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `package` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `package_manager` |

## Examples

Search for a package by name.

```nurt example
package.search "ripgrep"
```

Search one manager and keep the packages that are not installed.

```nurt example
package.search "editor" manager: apt |> filter installed == false
```

Show the first ten matches with their repositories.

```nurt example
package.search "json" |> first 10 |> select name version source
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
matched 330  shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | No supported package manager was found, or the given one is not installed. | Pass `manager` of an installed manager. |
| `E_FORMAT` | Every repository index of the given manager is unreadable. | Refresh the indexes with the manager. |
| `E_LIMIT` | The matches exceed the record limit. | Use a more specific query. |

## Related

`package.list`, `package.install`.

# package.upgrade

## Synopsis

```text
package.upgrade <names>... [name: value]...
```

## Description

`package.upgrade` upgrades the named packages, or all installed packages when no name is given, through the program of the package manager. The mark [P] in the catalog identifies this use of an external program. The program is started without a shell, with the arguments as a list, and with the variables of `run.env_defaults` followed by the variables of the manager that keep it non-interactive. No program is started during a preview.

The records list the packages that the local indexes show as outdated when no name is given. pacman upgrades named packages without the rest of the system, which is a partial upgrade; the command reports a warning in that case. With no name pacman runs a full system upgrade.

The command needs the privilege of the manager. apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the superuser and fail with `E_PRIVILEGE` otherwise; with `privilege: elevated` the call runs through an elevation backend (`sudo`, `doas`, `run0`, or in the same process when Nurt is the administrator), and the command itself never writes `sudo`. Homebrew refuses to run as the superuser and fails with `E_PRIVILEGE` in that case. When the lock of the package database is held, the command fails with `E_IN_USE` and lists the holding processes.

A non-zero exit code of the manager ends the command with `E_STAGE_FAILED` and the end of its error output. The effect is reported as executed in that case, because the manager may have changed packages before it failed.

**Privilege.** apt, dnf, pacman and zypper need the administrator; write `privilege: elevated` on the stage.

```nurt
package.upgrade ["jq"] privilege: elevated
```

`undo` of the entry installs the recorded versions again, when the repository still offers them.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `names` | `list<text>` | none | Packages to upgrade; all installed packages when omitted. |
| `manager` | `enum(auto\|apt\|dnf\|pacman\|zypper\|brew\|winget\|choco\|scoop)` | `auto` | Package manager; auto selects the manager of the system. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

The record of each package has `target` `package:<name>`, `action`, `before` (installed version, absent when the package was not installed) and `after` (version read from the package database after the run).

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `irreversible` |
| Implementation | `package_manager` |

## Examples

Upgrade all packages.

```nurt example
package.upgrade
```

Upgrade two packages.

```nurt example
package.upgrade "openssl" "curl"
```

Upgrade all packages of Scoop.

```nurt example
package.upgrade manager: scoop
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The program of the manager is not installed. | Install the manager or pass another `manager`. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The user lacks the privilege of the manager, or the manager refuses the superuser. | Run as root, or as a regular user for Homebrew. |
| `E_IN_USE` | The package database is locked by another process. | Wait for the listed processes to finish. |

title: parse
text:
# parse

## Synopsis

```text
line|match|content |> parse <pattern>
```

## Description

`parse` matches `pattern` against the text of each record and gives a `row`
record whose `cells` are the named groups of the match, as text; a group that
does not take part in the match is `null`. Groups are named with
`(?<name>…)`. The row keeps the `path` of its input record.

| Input | Text | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| `line` | `text` | one row for the first match, numbered by the line |
| `match` | `line`, the whole line of the match | one row for the first match, numbered by the line |
| `content` | `text` | one row per match, numbered by the line where the match starts |

Records the pattern does not match give no row. The stage is lazy and keeps
the header of the stream.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | `regex` | required | Pattern whose named groups become fields. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `line`, `match`, `content` | `row` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `transform` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Split log lines into a level and a message:

```nurt example
lines "/home/user/app.log" |> parse /(?<level>[A-Z]+) (?<message>.*)/
```

Read the settings of an environment file:

```nurt example
read "/home/user/app.env" |> parse /^(?<key>\w+)=(?<value>.*)$/m
```

Extract a name and a number from the lines found by a search:

```nurt example
search /port/ "/home/user/app.conf" |> parse /(?<name>\w+)\s*=\s*(?<value>\d+)/
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | the pattern has no named groups | name the groups, for example `(?<level>\w+)` |
| `E_REGEX` | the pattern does not compile | correct the pattern |
| `E_TYPE` | the input records are not `line`, `match` or `content` | read the text first with `lines`, `search` or `read` |

## Related

`split`, `search`, `lines`.

title: patch
text:
# patch

## Synopsis

```text
patch [<diff>] root: <path> (diff: <text> | from: <path>) [name: value]...
```

## Description

`patch` applies a diff in unified format, as written by `diff -u`, or in git
format, as written by `git diff`, to the files below `root`. The diff is
given as text in `diff` or read from the file `from`; exactly one of them is
required. Text outside the file sections, such as a commit message, is
skipped.

The whole diff is applied in memory before anything changes. A hunk is
placed at the line of its header, shifted by the offset of the previous
hunk; when the old lines are not there, they are searched for at increasing
distances. With `fuzz: n`, up to `n` context lines at each end of a hunk may
differ. A hunk that cannot be placed fails the whole command with
`E_PATCH_REJECTED`, and no file changes. Later file sections see the result
of earlier ones, and each file is written once with its final content, in
one operation that `undo` reverts as a whole.

Paths in the diff are relative to `root`; `strip: n` removes `n` leading
components, as `patch -p n` (git diffs need `strip: 1` for their `a/` and
`b/` prefixes; `rename` and `copy` lines lose one component less). Absolute
paths and paths with `..` are rejected.

A changed file keeps its encoding, byte order mark and line endings: a diff
with `lf` line endings applies to a file with `crlf` line endings, and added
lines take the line ending of the file. New files are written in UTF-8 with
the line endings of the diff, and missing directories are created.

Git headers create (`new file mode`), delete (`deleted file mode`), rename
(`rename from`, `rename to`) and copy (`copy from`, `copy to`) files. A
rename without a change of content renames the file; a rename with changes
writes the new file and deletes the old one. A file section without git
headers whose old file is missing and whose hunks only add lines creates the
file. As with GNU `patch`, a file that such a section empties is deleted when
the time stamp of its new side is the Unix epoch, which `diff -N` writes for
a missing file; otherwise the empty file is kept and reported as
`file_emptied`.

A git mode change (`old mode`, `new mode`) is applied to a file whose content
does not change. For a file whose content changes, and for a new file with
execute bits, the mode is not applied and the change carries the flag
`mode_not_applied`.

`reverse: true` undoes the changes the diff describes: added lines are
removed, created files are deleted and renames are reverted.

The text of every created and changed file of a known format is checked
after the patch is applied: a document format of the documents group,
otherwise a language of the code group. Only syntax errors that the previous
content did not have count; a file created by a rename is compared with the
file it is renamed from. With `validate: reject` such an error in any file
rolls the whole patch back with `E_ROLLED_BACK`; with `warn` it is reported
as a warning and the patch is kept; `off` skips the check. Deleted files and
mode changes are not checked, and without the documents and code groups
nothing is checked.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | `path` | required | Directory that the paths in the diff are relative to. |
| `diff` | `text` | one of `patch_source` | Diff text. |
| `from` | `path` | one of `patch_source` | File that contains the diff. |
| `reverse` | `bool` | `false` | Apply the diff in reverse. |
| `fuzz` | `int` | `0` | Number of context lines that may differ when a hunk is placed. |
| `strip` | `int` | `0` | Number of leading path components removed from the paths in the diff. |
| `validate` | `enum(off\|warn\|reject)` | `reject` | Roll back the change when it introduces a new syntax error. |
| `if_match` | `text \| map<text>` | none | Expected etag of the patched file, or a map from path to etag for several files; a different file is not changed. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

The `effect` record has one `change` per target in the order of execution:
created directories, renames, then the other files in path order. A change
of file content has `added`, `removed` and `diff` (the `hunk` records of the
change, with three lines of context); a changed file also has
`encoding_before`, `encoding_after`, `line_ending_before`,
`line_ending_after`, `bom_before` and `bom_after`. The flags `hunk_offset`
and `hunk_fuzz` mark a file whose hunks were placed at another line or with
ignored context lines.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `local` |
| Reversibility | `reversible` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

Notable entries: `unchanged` for a file the diff leaves as it is,
`file_emptied` for a file left empty, `encoding_preserved` and
`line_ending_preserved` for files written in an encoding other than UTF-8 or
with line endings other than `lf`.

## Examples

Apply a fix written by `git diff` to a project with `crlf` line endings.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/fix-timeout.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1
```

```text expected
op 41  patch  ok
targets 1 file
  ~ /srv/app/src/config.rs  +1 -1
```

Apply a git diff that creates, deletes and renames files.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/layout.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1
```

```text expected
op 42  patch  ok
targets 5
  + /srv/app/docs/
  + /srv/app/src/support/
  > /srv/app/src/util.rs -> /srv/app/src/support/util.rs
  - /srv/app/INSTALL.txt
  + /srv/app/docs/setup.md  +2
```

Undo the first example.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/fix-timeout.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1 reverse: true
```

A diff that no longer matches the file changes nothing.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/fix-timeout.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1
```

```text expected
error E_PATCH_REJECTED  stage 1  /srv/app/src/config.rs:1
  hunk 1 does not apply to src/config.rs at line 1; check the file version or raise fuzz
```

A diff that removes the closing brace of `package.json` is rolled back
together with its change of `README.md`.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/bump.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1
```

```text expected
error E_ROLLED_BACK  stage 1
  the change adds 1 syntax error to `/srv/app/package.json` and was rolled back: correct the new text or pass `validate: warn`
```

The same diff with `validate: warn` is applied, and the new error is
reported as a warning.

```nurt example
patch from: "/srv/patches/bump.diff" root: "/srv/app" strip: 1 validate: warn
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_PATCH_REJECTED` | A hunk does not match its file (`problem: hunk_rejected`, with the expected and actual lines and the location), or a file to delete has other content (`problem: delete_mismatch`). | Check the version of the file, adjust `strip`, or raise `fuzz`. |
| `E_FORMAT` | The diff is malformed, contains no file section, is a binary diff, names no file, has fewer path components than `strip`, or has an absolute path or a path with `..` (`problem` names the case). | Provide a text diff in unified or git format with paths relative to `root`. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | A file to change does not exist, or `root` or `from` does not exist. | Check `root` and `strip`. |
| `E_EXISTS` | A file to create already exists. | Remove the file, or apply the diff in reverse first. |
| `E_STALE` | A file does not have the etag of `if_match`, or changed after the plan. | Read the file again and repeat the call. |
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | Neither `diff` nor `from`, or no `root`. | Give the diff and the root directory. |
| `E_PARAM_CONFLICT` | Both `diff` and `from`. | Give one of them. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `strip` or `fuzz` is negative, `root` is not a directory (`problem: not_a_directory`), or a path of the diff is a directory or a link (`problem: not_a_file`). | Correct the value. |
| `E_UNKNOWN_VALUE` | `validate` is not `off`, `warn` or `reject`. | Use one of the listed values. |
| `E_ROLLED_BACK` | The patch adds a syntax error to a file and `validate` is `reject` (`problem: validate_failed`, one `sample` line per new error). | Correct the diff or pass `validate: warn`. |
| `E_BINARY` | A file to change has binary content. | Patch text files only. |
| `E_ENCODING` | A file is not valid in its detected encoding, or an added character cannot be represented in it. | Convert the file with `convert`. |
| `E_LIMIT` | A file is larger than the limit of text files. | Patch smaller files. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | A file cannot be read or written. | Check the permissions. |
| `E_IO` | A file cannot be read or written. | Check the permissions. |

## Related

`diff` returns the differences of files as `hunk` records. `replace`,
`insert` and `edit` change files by content instead of by line numbers.
`undo` reverts an applied patch.

title: ports
text:
# ports

## Synopsis

```text
ports [name: value]...
```

## Description

`ports` lists the TCP and UDP sockets of the host as `port` records, ordered
by protocol, local port, local address and process. With `state: listen` the
output holds listening TCP sockets and UDP sockets without a remote address;
with `state: all` it holds every socket, including established and closing
connections.

`local` is the local address and port as `address:port`, with an IPv6 address in
square brackets, for example `[::1]:8080`. `remote`, `remote_address` and
`remote_port` are set only for sockets with a peer. UDP sockets have the
state `none`. `pid` and `process` identify the process that holds the socket.

| System | Socket tables | Holding process |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `/proc/net/tcp`, `tcp6`, `udp`, `udp6` | descriptor in `/proc/<pid>/fd` that links to the socket inode |
| macOS | `proc_pidfdinfo(PROC_PIDFDSOCKETINFO)` for each process | the process listed |
| Windows | `GetExtendedTcpTable`, `GetExtendedUdpTable` | process identifier of the table row |

On Linux the holding process of a socket of another account is known only to
a privileged account; such sockets keep an empty `pid`. On macOS the sockets
of processes of other accounts are listed only for a privileged account. In
both cases the report carries one `source_unavailable` note with the number
of affected sockets or processes. TCP states map to `listen`, `established`,
`syn_sent`, `syn_received`, `fin_wait`, `close_wait`, `closing`, `last_ack`,
`time_wait` and `closed`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `state` | `enum(listen\|all)` | `listen` | Listening ports only, or all sockets. |
| `protocol` | `enum(tcp\|udp\|any)` | `any` | Transport protocol. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `port` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

List the listening TCP ports:

```nurt example
ports state: listen protocol: tcp
```

List all UDP sockets:

```nurt example
ports state: all protocol: udp
```

List all sockets with their states and processes:

```nurt example
ports state: all
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
matched 85  shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `state` or `protocol` has a value outside the enumeration. | Use one of the listed values. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The socket tables are not readable by the account. | Run with the privilege named in `required`. |
| `E_IO` | A socket table cannot be read. | Check the state of the system and run the program again. |

## Related

`processes`, `network.interfaces`, `open_files`.

title: power.cancel
text:
# power.cancel

## Synopsis

```text
power.cancel
```

## Description

`power.cancel` cancels a scheduled restart or shutdown with `shutdown -c` on Linux, `shutdown /a` on Windows and by stopping `shutdown` on macOS. On Linux the schedule is read from `/run/systemd/shutdown/scheduled`; without one the command reports `unchanged`. A cancelled schedule is not restored by `undo`.

Rights: the command accepts `privilege`; write `privilege: elevated` when the account that runs Nurt is not the administrator. A program that fails for lack of rights ends the command with `E_PERMISSION`, and `privilege: auto` repeats it once elevated. An elevated entry is undone by the same elevated process.

`undo` reports that the cancelled schedule is not restored.

## Parameters

The command has no parameters.

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `irreversible` |
| Implementation | `system_program` |
| Reversibility conditions | A cancelled schedule is not restored. |
| External use | `system_program`: `shutdown`, `pkill`; The schedule is cancelled with shutdown -c on Linux, shutdown /a on Windows and by stopping shutdown on macOS. |

## Examples

Cancel the schedule.

```nurt example
power.cancel privilege: elevated
```

Run the cancellation with elevated rights; adding the call parameter `preview: true` shows the effect first.

```nurt example
power.cancel privilege: elevated
```

Cancel and show the effect.

```nurt example
power.cancel privilege: elevated |> select target
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | Nothing is scheduled (Windows). | No action is needed. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The account lacks the rights of the administrator. | Add `privilege: elevated`. |
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The system program of the command is not installed. | Install the program named in the message. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The system program ended with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`power.restart`, `power.shutdown`.

title: power.restart
text:
# power.restart

## Synopsis

```text
power.restart [name: value]...
```

## Description

`power.restart` restarts the system with `shutdown`. Without `at` and `delay` the action runs at once and is irreversible; the report says so before the change. With `at` (an instant, converted to a delay with the clock of the engine) or `delay` (rounded up to whole minutes on Linux and macOS) the action is scheduled and `power.cancel` undoes it. A second schedule while one exists is `E_IN_USE` on Linux. `message` is shown to the logged-in users.

Rights: the command accepts `privilege`; write `privilege: elevated` when the account that runs Nurt is not the administrator. A program that fails for lack of rights ends the command with `E_PERMISSION`, and `privilege: auto` repeats it once elevated. An elevated entry is undone by the same elevated process.

`undo` of a scheduled action runs `power.cancel`; an immediate action cannot be undone.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `at` | `instant` | none | Time of the restart; converted to a delay with the clock of the engine. |
| `delay` | `duration` | none | Time until the restart; rounded up to whole minutes on Linux and macOS. |
| `message` | `text` | none | Message shown to the logged-in users. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `effect` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `change` |
| Effect | `external` |
| Reversibility | `reversible_if_preserved` |
| Implementation | `system_program` |
| Reversibility conditions | A scheduled restart is undone by power.cancel; one without at or delay runs at once and is irreversible. |
| External use | `system_program`: `shutdown`; The system is restarted with the program shutdown. |

## Examples

Schedule in ten minutes.

```nurt example
power.restart delay: 10m message: "Maintenance" privilege: elevated
```

Schedule at a time.

```nurt example
power.restart at: "2026-12-01T03:00:00Z" privilege: elevated
```

Run the immediate action with elevated rights; adding the call parameter `preview: true` shows the effect first.

```nurt example
power.restart privilege: elevated
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_IN_USE` | A restart or shutdown is already scheduled. | Cancel it with `power.cancel`. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `at` is in the past. | Give a later time. |
| `E_PERMISSION` | The account lacks the rights of the administrator. | Add `privilege: elevated`. |
| `E_EXTERNAL_MISSING` | The system program of the command is not installed. | Install the program named in the message. |
| `E_STAGE_FAILED` | The system program ended with an error. | Read the end of the error output in the message. |

## Related

`power.cancel`, `power.restart`, `power.shutdown`.

title: processes
text:
# processes

## Synopsis

```text
processes [<name>] [name: value]...
```

## Description

`processes` lists the processes of the host as `process` records, ordered by
`pid`. `name`, `user` and `pid` select processes; all given conditions must
hold. A text `name` matches the whole process name, and on Windows also the
name followed by `.exe`; a regular expression matches any part of the name.
`user` matches the account name or the account identifier (`uid`).

With `tree: true` the selected processes are the roots of a tree. The output
holds each root followed by all its descendants in depth-first order,
children ordered by `pid`, with the fields `depth` (0 for a root) and
`children`. A selected process that descends from another selected process
appears once, under its ancestor. Without conditions the roots are the
processes whose parent is not in the table. Parent links that form a cycle
are cut at the repeated process and reported as a warning.

`cpu` is the processor use in percent of one core. When the rest of the
pipeline names the fields it uses and `cpu` is among them, the command reads
the processor time twice, 200 ms apart, and reports the use in that interval.
Otherwise `cpu` is the average over the lifetime of the process, computed
from one reading without waiting. A process that ends between the two
readings is left out; a process that starts between them has no `cpu`.

`memory` is the resident memory. `uid` is the effective user identifier on
Linux and macOS and the security identifier of the process token on Windows.
`cwd` is read only with `cwd: true`. Without input conditions the command
reads the table lazily, so a following limit stops the reading early.

| Data | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| process table | `/proc/<pid>/stat`, `status` | `proc_listpids`, `proc_pidinfo` | Toolhelp snapshot |
| `command` | `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` | `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)` | process environment block |
| `executable` | `/proc/<pid>/exe` | `proc_pidpath` | `QueryFullProcessImageNameW` |
| `cwd` | `/proc/<pid>/cwd` | `PROC_PIDVNODEPATHINFO` | process environment block |
| `state` | state letter of `stat` | `pbi_status` | always `running` |

Fields of processes of other accounts that the account may not read, such as
`executable`, `command` and `cwd`, stay empty. The report carries one
`source_unavailable` note with the number of such processes. On Linux a
kernel thread has an empty `command` and its name in square brackets, for
example `[kthreadd]`. A state without a counterpart is `other`, and
`os_raw.state` holds the code of the system.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text \| regex` | none | Process name or pattern. |
| `user` | `text` | none | Only processes of this account. |
| `pid` | `int` | none | Only the process with this identifier. |
| `cwd` | `bool` | `false` | Include the working directory of each process. |
| `tree` | `bool` | `false` | Return processes as a tree with child lists and depth. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `process` |

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

List the processes named `nginx` with their child processes:

```nurt example
processes name: "nginx" tree: true
```

List the processes of one account with their working directories:

```nurt example
processes user: "www-data" cwd: true
```

Show one process by its identifier:

```nurt example
processes pid: 1
```

Select processes by a pattern of the name:

```nurt example
processes /^python[0-9.]*$/
```

A response that leaves records out ends with the hint "more: next" and carries the field
`continuation`; the command `next` returns the next part without running the
command again.

```text
matched 410  shown 50  more: next
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `name` is not a valid regular expression, or `pid` is negative. | Correct the pattern or the identifier. |
| `E_PRIVILEGE` | The process table is not readable by the account. | Run with the privilege named in `required`. |
| `E_IO` | The process table cannot be read, for example `/proc` is not mounted. | Mount `proc` at `/proc`. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | The execution was cancelled during the measurement of `cpu`. | Run the program again. |

## Related

`ports`, `open_files`, `suspend`, `resume`, `stop`.

title: program.catalog
text:
# program.catalog

## Synopsis

```text
program.catalog [<category>] [name: value]...
```

## Description

`program.catalog` lists the programs of the index by category. It starts a pipeline and accepts no input.

Without `category` the result is one `program_category` record per category that holds at least one program, ordered by the number of programs descending and then by id. Categories come from the built-in taxonomy and from external catalogs; a catalog category with the id of a built-in category, or one that declares it in `same_as`, is the same category. Programs of the computer are placed by their desktop entry, package section or group, manual page section and, failing those, by a keyword classifier; `category_source` on each card tells which.

With `category` and a category divided into subcategories, the result is one `program_category` record per subcategory with programs, in catalog order, followed by the subcategory `_other` for the programs outside every subcategory. With a category without subcategories, or with `subcategory`, the result is the `program_card` records of its programs ordered by name. `subcategory` accepts the id or an alias of the subcategory, and `_other`.

With `query` the programs of the category are ranked as by `program.search` and at most 30 are emitted; `subcategory` is then ignored.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `category` | `text` | none | Category to open; without it the result lists all categories. |
| `subcategory` | `text` | none | Subcategory to open. |
| `query` | `text` | none | Keywords that narrow the listed programs. |
| `source` | `text` | none | Only programs from this source. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `program_category`, `program_card` |

Records of `program_category` carry the additional fields `level` (`category` or `subcategory`), `parent`, `summary`, `aliases`, `sources` and `counts_by_source`.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

List the categories of the programs of the computer.

```nurt example
program.catalog
```

```text expected
name      count  title
system    412    System and administration
code      138    Development
network   57     Network
```

Open one category and show its programs.

```nurt example
program.catalog "archives" |> select name summary
```

Rank the programs of a category from one catalog.

```nurt example
program.catalog "video" query: "subtitles" source: "catalog" |> first 5
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | The category is unknown or holds no program; `candidates` lists the nearest categories. | Use a listed category. |
| `E_ARG` | `subcategory` was given without `category`, the category has no subcategories, the subcategory is unknown, or the query is shorter than 2 or longer than 200 characters. | Pass `category`, omit `subcategory`, or use a listed subcategory. |
| `E_CATALOG` | `source` names a program catalog that is not configured or cannot be read. | Check `programs.catalogs`. |

## Related

`program.search`, `program.describe`, `program.find`.

title: program.describe
text:
# program.describe

## Synopsis

```text
program.describe <name> [name: value]...
```

## Description

`program.describe` emits one `program_card` record with the full description of a program, application or usage guide. It starts a pipeline and accepts no input.

The name is looked up in the program index: first as a card name, then as an alias (a symbolic link in `PATH`, a Debian alternative, a shim of Scoop or Chocolatey, an application execution alias, or an alias declared by a catalog), then as the name of a standalone guide of a catalog. For an alias the record describes the main program; the field `requested` holds the given name and `alias_kind` the kind of alias. On Windows and macOS names are compared without regard to case.

The record merges every provider that knows the program: path and alternatives from `PATH`, version, homepage, licence and package description from the package database, application name and identifier from the application entry, the `NAME` line of the manual page in the field `man`, and description, situations of use, tasks the program is not meant for, an example, pitfalls and the usage guide from external catalogs. `guide_sections` lists the headings of the guide; `etag` identifies the content of the record and `guide_etag` that of the guide. Programs that share one guide list each other in `guide_shared_with`.

With a list of names the command emits one record per name that exists and reports the others as warnings; it fails with `E_NOT_FOUND` only when no name exists. `section` selects one section of the guide by heading, `query` the sections of the guide that match its words, and `include_guide: false` leaves the guide out. When `unchanged_since` equals the `etag` of the record, the record carries `unchanged: true` and nothing else of the description. `source` restricts the lookup to the listed sources, named as in `program.catalog`.

The help text of a program is never read on its own: `program.describe` starts no program unless `help: true` is given. The program then runs once with `--help` within the time limit `programs.help_timeout`, and its output is returned in the field `help`.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `text \| list<text>` | required | Program name, or up to 12 names. |
| `include_guide` | `bool` | `true` | Include the usage guide when one is available. |
| `section` | `text` | none | Return only the section of the guide with this heading. |
| `query` | `text` | none | Return only the sections of the guide that match these keywords. |
| `unchanged_since` | `text` | none | Etag of an earlier record; an unchanged program returns only unchanged. |
| `source` | `text \| list<text>` | none | Only programs from these sources. |
| `help` | `bool` | `false` | Run the program once with --help and return its output in the field help. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `program_card` |

The record carries the fields of `program_card` and, when they apply, `kind`, `etag`, `requested`, `alias_kind`, `description`, `when_to_use`, `not_for`, `example`, `pitfalls`, `man`, `guide`, `guide_sections`, `guide_files`, `guide_etag` and `guide_shared_with`.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |
| External use | `user_program`; used when `help` is given; Runs the program once with --help, with a time limit, to read its help text. |

## Examples

Describe an installed program.

```nurt example
program.describe "tar"
```

```text expected
name  category  version  path          summary
tar   archives  1.35     /usr/bin/tar  An archiving utility.
```

Describe a program whose guide was already read in the session.

```nurt example
program.describe "ffmpeg" include_guide: false |> select name guide_sections guide_etag
```

Resolve an alias to its main program.

```nurt example
program.describe "vi" |> select name requested alias_kind path
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | No name was given. | Pass a program name. |
| `E_INVALID_VALUE` | The name is longer than 120 characters. | Pass the program name without arguments. |
| `E_NOT_FOUND` | No program, application or guide has the name; `candidates` lists up to eight similar names. | Use a candidate, or find the program with `program.search`. |

## Related

`program.search`, `program.find`, `program.catalog`.

title: program.find
text:
# program.find

## Synopsis

```text
program.find <name>... [name: value]...
```

## Description

`program.find` resolves each name in the directories of `PATH` in the order the operating system uses and emits one `program_location` record per name, in the order of the arguments. It starts a pipeline and accepts no input. Repeated names are reported once.

A name that resolves gives `found: true`, the first matching file in `path` and, with `all`, every match in `all_paths`. A name that does not resolve gives a record with `found: false` and no path; the command does not fail. On Windows the extensions of `PATHEXT` are tried in order and names are compared without regard to case; on macOS names are compared without regard to case; on Linux and other Unix systems the comparison is exact and only files with an execute permission are matched. A symbolic link in `PATH` that points to another program in `PATH` is reported with the field `alias_of`.

A name that contains a path separator, such as `./tool` or `bin/tool`, is not searched in `PATH`; the file is checked as it is, a relative name relative to the base directory of the request.

`program.find` reads only the directories of `PATH`; it does not build the program index unless `versions` is `true`. With `versions` the version comes from the program index: from the package database, the application entry or a catalog, and `version_source` names which of `package`, `app` or `catalog` gave it. No program is started; a located program without a version in these sources has none.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `list<text>` | required | Program names. |
| `versions` | `bool` | `false` | Read the version of each located program. |
| `all` | `bool` | `false` | List every match in all_paths. |

## Input and output

| Form | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| default | `none` | `program_location` |

Fields of `program_location`: `name`, `found`, `path`, `all_paths`, `version`, `source`, and the additional fields `alias_of` and `version_source` when they apply.

## Effect

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | `source` |
| Effect | `read` |
| Reversibility | `read` |
| Implementation | `builtin` |

## Examples

Locate two programs.

```nurt example
program.find "git" "rg"
```

```text expected
name  found  path
git   true   /usr/bin/git
rg    true   /usr/local/bin/rg
```

Report the names that are not installed.

```nurt example
program.find "ffmpeg" "gs" "magick" |> filter found == false |> select name
```

Show the installed version of each program with its source.

```nurt example
program.find "python3" "node" versions: true |> select name version version_source
```

## Errors

| Code | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `E_MISSING_PARAM` | No name was given. | Pass at least one program name. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | The execution was cancelled while names were being resolved. | Run the command again. |

## Related

`program.search`, `program.describe`, `program.catalog`.

title: program.search
text:
# program.search

## Synopsis

```text
program.search <query> [name: value]...
```
